covenants.name: Aedes Veritatis
covenants.notes:
Its people. The magi are three: 'Umar, the leader; Amber, his friend and second; and Wardat, the youngest, whom 'Umar sponsored into the Order. Of the twenty specialists and 150 grogs, most are men-at-arms, and the covenant has the air of a garrison.

covenants.summary:
Counter-Crusader: the leader of the magi who would fight the Crusader covenants for the Muslims' sake.

Bayt al-Haqq in Arabic, the House of Truth, a name that also means the house of what is right. A sandstone fortress on a mountain top east of Damascus, founded in 1112 by Maryam al-Dimashqiyya, a young Jerbiton maga of that city, as a stronghold for the magi who had taken the Muslims' side against their Hermetic brothers. Good management and quick work on its walls and its friendships made it the bastion of the counter-Crusade. Maryam fell at Hattin in 1187, with most of the covenant's magi, and her filius Sharaf al-Din 'Umar has led it since. Its device is a stylised house holding the Arabic word haqq.

The fortress was built for war: thick stone walls with arrow slits and battlements, a watchtower jutting from the north-west corner that also houses the magi, and a great hall in the middle where the grogs train more often than anyone feasts. Its neighbours take it for the seat of some reclusive emir, a part 'Umar plays when he must. Its income is stone from a quarry near by, sold in Damascus, where it buys most of what it needs; some covenants asked whether stone for walls was help in the war, and the quaesitores ruled the trade lawful.

Magi: 'Umar, Amber the Golden of Tremere and the sahira Wardat al-Quds; the book counts four, and names no fourth.

covenants.name: Domus Pacis
covenants.notes:
The khan. A high wall closes a central courtyard, with two storeys of buildings against it: on the ground floor the smithy and the merchants' rooms and storerooms, above them most of the grogs and covenfolk. The cave system beneath, where the magi live, is lit and aired by enchanted devices.

Suggested vis sources (not in the book), for the storyguide to use, change or ignore: the dew that gathers on the cliff face over the khan on the mornings after a meeting has ended (Rego, 3 pawns); a spring deep in the caves whose water tastes of whatever the drinker last dreamt (Mentem, 2 pawns); and the soot of the smithy's forge on the night of the winter solstice (Ignem, 2 pawns).
covenants.summary:
Mediator: neutral ground, and the seat of the Tribunal.

Dar al-Salam to its neighbours, the Abode of Peace: a roadside khan north of Jerusalem where merchants put up for the night, paying fees that are part of the covenant's income. The grogs and covenfolk live in the rooms round the courtyard; the magi and the rest of the grogs live in caves hidden under the inn. Its device is a hand.

Aurora of Jerbiton founded it in 1169, with Tau of Flambeau's help, as a place where magi of the Order and wizards of other traditions could meet and trade knowledge. She has moved on, but the covenant keeps to her purpose: Hermetic magi, raqis and other mages still come to talk over their work. Since Tau became Praeco it is also the Tribunal's meeting place. Every seven years tents go up outside the khan for the visitors, the main gate is shut and opened only for magi coming to the meeting, and inside chairs are set in a ring in the courtyard where the business is argued and decided.

The warlike magi of the Tribunal think little of it, and it is poorly defended; perhaps only its enemies' contempt and their fear of its powerful friends have spared it worse. Its magi are energetic, though, and may soon set its troubles right.

Magi: Tau, Felix of Guernicus and Esther of Verditius; the book counts four, and names no fourth.

A Hermetic Military Order?: zealous magi, chafing at the peace with the Muslims, mean to found a military order of their own in the hope that papal blessing will shield them from the quaesitores, and camp on the characters' doorstep demanding they join.
covenants.summary:
Crusader: the loudest of the covenants that want the old war on the Muslims back.

Not the oldest Crusader covenant, but the one that leads them. Its founders, the Flambeau Guillaume de Bourne and the Tytalus Rufus de Clary, two Frenchmen as violent as they are unruly, came to the Levant in 1188, just after Salah al-Din took Jerusalem, and set up their covenant to be the Order's lasting foothold on the coast, hence its name. Its device is a flaming sword; it is affiliated with House Flambeau.

A two-storey stone keep in a yard, inside a strong wall with battlements and a parapet, on a hill inland from the coast between Acre and Tyre. Grogs and servants live on both floors, the magi on the upper one only. Two fishermen and a merchant among the specialists keep it supplied by selling fish and what timber is cut. The covenfolk are mostly French and mostly loyal to their masters and their cause, though there has been some grumbling in the ranks. The magi, lost in dreams of conquest, neglect their household, and it may take an attack to wake them.

The other Crusader covenants back it and the counter-Crusaders hate it. The quaesitores see it as the chief danger to a shaky peace and suspect its magi of crusading still. If the Treaty ever fails, Foothold may well be the first to fall.

covenants.name: The Hermetic Embassy
covenants.notes:
The house. A Muslim-style town house with a council chamber, closed in by the city on every side; a neighbour's roof looks down into it from the south.

Suggested vis sources (not in the book), for the storyguide to use, change or ignore: ink scraped from a treaty the caliph's chancery has sealed and then cancelled (Rego, 2 pawns); the reflection in the house's fountain at the moment the call to prayer falls silent at sunset, caught in a glass bowl (Imaginem, 2 pawns); and the down of a pigeon from the caliph's post lofts that has flown the road from Damascus a hundred times (Corpus, 1 pawn).

Story seeds:
A Strike at the Heart: a meeting of the Tribunal throws out the Treaty and plans to cripple the caliph's mages by killing their leaders in Baghdad; the Crusader magi press the characters to take part and suspect any who hesitate, and pro-Muslim covenants such as Aedes Veritatis are among the first to be Renounced.
covenants.summary:
Mediator: the keeper of the Treaty of Baghdad.

The Order's presence in Baghdad: a house built in the Muslim manner in the quarter of al-Qurayya, near the caliph's palace, where two magi live with their bodyguards and servants and look after the Treaty and the Order's standing at the courts of the caliph and the Ayyubid sultans. Aurora of Jerbiton founded it in 1193, when she became a quaesitor, to watch over the peace she had made. Its device is a white flag with the sign of the Order.

Magvillus, the domus magna of House Guernicus, pays for it, so it is affiliated with that House, though no Guernicus magus lives there. Its two magi have proved devoted to its purpose and are left to themselves.

Foothold and Aedes Veritatis, the leaders of the two warring factions, harass it now and then with indirect and political attacks. None has come to violence, and none is likely to, given Aurora's standing and the quaesitores' weight; but if the Treaty were abandoned its magi would have to leave the city at once. The Suhhar Sulayman of Baghdad, who never signed the Treaty, distrust it.

covenants.name: Urbs Rubra
covenants.summary:
Aloof: its two magi take no part in Tribunal business at all.

The Red City, the Tribunal's oldest covenant, founded in 802 by the caliph Harun al-Rashid's leave, in the ancient city of Petra, from which it takes its name. A deep gorge opens onto a meeting of valleys full of caves, rooms and buildings cut or raised over the centuries by the Nabataeans, the Romans and the Byzantines; last came the Crusaders, who built a castle on a hill deep inside and left it soon after Hattin. The covenant is now mostly left alone. Its device is three red houses; it is affiliated with House Criamon.

Its magi are Fade and Wraith of Criamon, husband and wife, the eldest in the Tribunal. A band of jinn living in great blocks of stone in the entrance gorge serves and guards them, and has grown so protective of its failing masters that it turns every visitor away; some of these jinn are too strong for any Hermetic magus to force a way past. No one has seen the pair for years, which is why the quaesitores ruled Tau the eldest in 1207.

The second covenant of the Tribunal, founded in 806, a network of caves high in two bleached cliffs in the Alan lands, which has outlasted the region's wars by being out of the way. Its device is a mountain with two peaks.

Its magi study a people of faeries near by, the Genjii, who are so like the jinn that the covenant's leader, Selene of Merinita, thinks the two have a common ancestor. She cannot yet prove it, and a pact with the Genjii that forbids her to pry too far into their secrets may mean she never will.

The book describes it as it was before the adventure The Sorcerer's Slave, set late in the thirteenth century, which has other magi and more of its layout and its dealings with the Genjii.

Crusader: it backs Foothold's call to fight on against the Muslims, and otherwise keeps to itself.

For War, also called the Covenant of Lions: a fortress hidden in the Sinai desert, set up in 1099 as soon as the First Crusade was won, to shelter Hermetic magi and to train House Flambeau's young fighters; it is affiliated with that House. Its device is a gold lion rampant on red.

Two firm friends lead it, Tiberius of Flambeau and Leo of Bjornaer. It owes its other name to lions: Leo's heartbeast is one and he keeps several as companions, Tiberius's familiar is a lion called Atlas, and two magically animated lion statues guard the fortress. The two seniors are glad to spread so noble a picture. It cares little for the Tribunal's politics. The quaesitores suspect its magi, as they do Foothold's, of fighting in the Crusaders' battles, but have proved nothing.

Being far more remote than Domus Pacis, and on far richer vis, it still has all the vis trade with Rome, but it wants its old supremacy back. It bears the other magi of Domus Pacis no grudge, but would help anyone hostile to Esther if it thought it could get away with it.

covenants.summary:
Messengers: the Tribunal's Redcaps, who take no side.

A covenant on the move: a caravan of House Mercere, with which it is affiliated, going from covenant to covenant across the Tribunal and calling on each about twice a year. It is no train of carts in the western way, which are rare in these lands, but a long string of camels, horses and asses laden with tents, rugs and camping gear and with the belongings of the Redcaps and their grogs, travelling by day and camping at night. Its device is a scroll under House Mercere's seal.

Of its five Redcaps only Simon is Gifted. He usually stays with the caravan, making magic items to help his fellows on the road; he has become expert at setting up a working laboratory in the unlikeliest places, and a howdah on one of his camels serves as the place for work that must be left to stand. The caravan's beasts are trained not to shy at magic. His twin sister Sarah, who guards him too closely, also keeps to the caravan; the other three are mostly away, carrying messages that cannot wait for the next visit.

covenants.name: The Pyramids (I)
covenants.summary:
Aloof: its magi care for nothing but the pyramids.

The first of the book's two covenants at the pyramids of Giza, which it offers as alternatives, or, for the bold, both at once, since the second lies in a regio: the troupe chooses. This one is a camp of tents near the Great Pyramid, where Ruth of Bonisagus and Pariah of Criamon live with their grogs. Its device is a pyramid.

Both magi are obsessed with the pyramids. They have mastered the restless spirits of the place and use them to learn the pyramids' history and to keep intruders off; they are trying to read the hieroglyphs on the walls of the burial chamber of the greatest pyramid and to find a way into the others, hoping for the hidden wisdom of the ancients and a way past the limits of Hermetic magic. Their single-mindedness unsettles other magi, and no one knows how far they will go, or what they might let loose if another pyramid opens.

The second of the book's two covenants at Giza, offered as an alternative to the first or alongside it, since it lies in a regio: the troupe chooses. Since ancient times a brotherhood of twelve priests and priestesses of Thoth and Anubis has worshipped in a temple hidden in a regio near the pyramids and the Sphinx. When one died, another Gifted soul was drawn to the temple to take the place, so they were always twelve. Its device is the hieroglyphs of the two gods; it is affiliated with House Ex Miscellanea.

In 1177 a priest died and the one drawn in was a respected Hermetic scholar, Heliobus Magister of Bonisagus, just as Hermetic magi had begun raiding the temple for its magical wealth. He soon had the priesthood admitted to House Ex Miscellanea, in 1178, which put it under the Code and ended the raids, and its worship goes on in peace.

So far Heliobus seems to care only for studying his fellows' rites, but the Tribunal's political covenants worry that he controls twelve votes; if he ever chose to use them he would be a power. And nobody knows what magic the temple hides.

They have called on the Order for others to join them, but few are likely to come until Damietta is safer. Its device is a cross.

tribunals.name: The Levant Tribunal
tribunals.summary:
The Order's easternmost Tribunal, reaching from Trebizond and the Alan lands of the Caucasus through Lesser Armenia, Syria and the four Latin states to Cyprus, Egypt and Sinai, and east to Baghdad. It began as the Tribunal of the East, two covenants (Urbs Rubra at Petra in 802 and Urania in the Caucasus in 806) founded by Harun al-Rashid's leave, won through Charlemagne's embassies, and reckoned a Tribunal in 832. Magi of every House came after the First Crusade, staked out territories over the old covenants' protests, and the Grand Tribunal of 1129 recognised the refounded Tribunal under its new name.

A young Tribunal in every sense. It is dangerous, so its magi are young and few live to old age; few covenants pass spring or summer, and one that reaches autumn is honoured for it. The Order's hold is slight and a magus can stay independent with ease. For most of a century magi meddled in the wars, fought the Muslims' mages, and turned on one another in Wizard Wars over the land's riches, with quaesitores as deep in it as anyone, until the Treaty of Baghdad of 1193 brought a hard peace. There are fifteen covenants and fifty-nine magi, about forty-eight of them in covenants. Flambeau, Verditius, Criamon and Jerbiton are the commonest Houses, then Tremere and Tytalus; Merinita is rarest, for want of faeries, and few of the land's own wizards join Ex Miscellanea.

Its questions. Crusade and jihad first: the Treaty forbids both, the quaesitores enforce it as best they can, and others hunt for loopholes or meddle unseen. Each covenant takes a stance, which its summary gives first: Crusader (Foothold, Para Belli and their allies, who want war on the Muslims), counter-Crusader (Aedes Veritatis and its allies, who want war on Foothold), mediator (the Hermetic Embassy, Domus Pacis and the quaesitores, who keep the Treaty), trader, or aloof. Then the border with Thebes, settled on paper and quick to flare; trade with Rome and, against the quaesitores' efforts, with merchants, churchmen and lords, chiefly by Jerbiton and Verditius magi; and the old wisdom of the East, which Criamon and Jerbiton magi seek among the ruins and from the land's mages and Sufis.

The meeting. Since Tau of Flambeau became Praeco the Tribunal has met every seven years at his covenant, Domus Pacis, a khan north of Jerusalem: tents go up outside for the visitors, the gate is shut to all but magi, and the business is done from a ring of chairs in the courtyard. The last meetings were in 1207 and 1214, and the next, in 1221, must vote on renewing the Treaty; the book gives no season, so summer is assumed. The chair must be a quaesitor of House Guernicus, a rule Aurora proposed so that she would never have to preside and be called partial; Scipio of Guernicus holds it now and keeps no covenant. Votes are one to a magus, which gives Heliobus of the Pyramids twelve.

Playing in the Levant. The book offers the troupe a part as mediators, between the Tribunal's factions or between the Order and the caliph and the Ayyubids: whether they succeed or not, they will make friends and enemies inside the Order and out.

Stories. The book frames the saga as the Treaty of Baghdad under strain: the Crusade at Damietta has the Crusader magi calling for war, the counter-Crusaders fight them in secret, and the mediators struggle to keep the peace. Under way in 1220 are the vote on renewing the Treaty at the meeting of 1221 and Aedes Veritatis's secret war on Foothold, with the Fifth Crusade and the Mongol Conquest beyond the Order. Others wait for the storyguide: 'Umar's double loyalty, Esther's trade, Rufus's hoard, Amber against her House, Aurora's Twilight and the Embassy's succession, Fade and Wraith, Heliobus's bloc, the Theban border, Arash, the True Cross's call and the opening of the pyramids. The book's smaller story seeds sit on the places, covenants, magi and creatures they use.

cases.title: Renew the Treaty of Baghdad for 1223
cases.brought_by: The Hermetic Embassy, Domus Pacis and Aedes Veritatis
cases.against: Foothold, Para Belli and The True Cross
cases.charge:
That the Tribunal renew the Treaty of Baghdad for ten years from 1223, when its present term ends. The mediators bring it; the counter-Crusaders of Aedes Veritatis back it, as the Treaty shields the Muslims. The Crusader covenants want it rejected this time so that they can help the Crusade at Damietta, and both sides are hunting for votes. The aloof covenants are undecided, and Heliobus's twelve votes may settle it.

If it passes, give the ruling a term of seven years: it then ends at the meeting of 1228, the last before the Treaty lapses again in 1233, and comes back on the docket in time.
cases.evidence:
The Treaty of Baghdad and its two renewals
The Crusade at Damietta, and the strain it puts on the peace

cases.title: The slaying of a Crusader magus
cases.charge: Early in his career 'Umar fought and killed a Crusader magus who had attacked him. He would plead self-defence, but no one else saw it, so the slaying of a sodalis may be laid against him as a High Crime. Foothold has learnt of it and asks that he be Renounced, which would cost the counter-Crusaders their leader.

rulings.title: The Treaty of Baghdad
rulings.says: Made between the Order in the Levant and the caliph's court, with Salah al-Din's mages and their Ayyubid heirs, and forced on the Levant's magi at the meeting of 1193 by quaesitores from Magvillus. No magus may take any part in Crusade or jihad, for either side; the Order's fighting with the Muslims' mages is over; and a magus found meddling in the wars is severely punished. Aurora of Jerbiton made it, treating with the caliph, Salah al-Din and their mages from 1183. The Order of Suleiman as a body never signed it.

rulings.title: The Treaty's term
rulings.says: Muslim law lets a truce last ten years at most, so the Treaty lapses each decade unless the Tribunal renews it, and it is debated at every meeting. Each renewal is voted at the last meeting before the Treaty lapses; the present term runs to 1223, and its renewal is before the meeting of 1221.

rulings.title: The Treaty renewed for 1203
rulings.says: The meeting of 1200 renewed the Treaty for ten years from 1203.

rulings.title: The Treaty renewed for 1213
rulings.says: The meeting of 1207 renewed the Treaty, by a narrow vote, for ten years from 1213.

rulings.title: The chair
rulings.says: The quaesitor who presides at a meeting of the Tribunal must be of House Guernicus; a quaesitor of any other House may not. Aurora of Jerbiton proposed the rule.

rulings.title: The Praeco
rulings.says: Fade and Wraith of Urbs Rubra, the eldest magi, had not been seen for years and could not be reached, so the quaesitores ruled that Tau of Flambeau be held the eldest, and Praeco.

rulings.title: The stone of Aedes Veritatis
rulings.says: Some covenants asked whether Aedes Veritatis's sale of quarry stone to Damascus aided the war, since the stone might build walls. The quaesitores ruled the trade lawful: the stone is not magical, and was not made for war.

rulings.title: Enchanted devices
rulings.says: Selling enchanted devices to mundane lords is interference in mundane affairs, and forbidden.

rulings.title: The border with Thebes
rulings.says: After 1204 Theban magi followed the Byzantine refugees east and Thebes claimed more of Asia Minor for them; Aurora and other quaesitores of both Tribunals settled the quarrel short of war. The Empire of Nicaea belongs to the Theban Tribunal and the Empire of Trebizond to the Levant. Both sides have agreed to differ, and many are unhappy with it.

rulings.title: The priests of the Pyramids
rulings.says: Heliobus Magister of Bonisagus brought the twelve priests of Thoth and Anubis in their temple at Giza into House Ex Miscellanea, under the Code's protection, which ended the Hermetic raids on their temple.

rulings.title: Sahirs in the Order
rulings.says: A sahir may join the Order as any hedge wizard does, through House Ex Miscellanea, swearing the Oath and taking the Parma Magica.

diary.title: The Order of Hermes founded
diary.details: The Order is founded in the west, far from the lands that will one day be the Levant Tribunal. At this time Baghdad, built five years before by the caliph al-Mansur, is the young capital of the 'Abbasids.

diary.title: Urbs Rubra founded at Petra
diary.details:
Harun al-Rashid, caliph since 786, has been trading embassies with Charlemagne, a king with more friends in the Order than the quaesitores like to own. Through them the Order wins the caliph's leave for two covenants in his lands, and the first, Urbs Rubra, is raised among the rock-cut halls of Petra. Harun's reign is an age of wonders, when jinn and men in some places live side by side and trade with one another, and the caliph himself is said to take lessons in Hermetic magic.

Secrets
If the storyguide wants it, the rumour is true: Harun learnt the Order's magic and passed it to mages of his court, and their pupils' pupils practise it still (see the Islamic Tradition's story seeds).

diary.title: Urania founded in the Caucasus
diary.details: The second covenant by Harun's leave is made in caves high on two pale cliffs in the Alan country, north-east of the Black Sea. Its remoteness will keep it alive through every war to come.

diary.title: Harun dies, and the East forgets the Order
diary.details: Harun's sons fall to civil war over his throne, the Muslim world turns its eyes inward and later breaks into rival states, and the two covenants lose their friends at court. For almost three centuries the East is a quiet corner of the Order.

diary.title: House Ex Miscellanea joins the Order
diary.details: The hedge wizards' House is admitted, the road by which the Levant's priests of the Pyramids and its sahirs will one day come into the Order.

diary.title: The Tribunal of the East
diary.details: The lands of Urbs Rubra and Urania are counted a Tribunal of the Order and named the Tribunal of the East, since the Order has reached no further in that direction. (Ch02 says only that this came soon after the covenants were founded; 832 is the timeline's year.)

diary.title: The Sundering of House Tremere
diary.details: The timeline marks the Sundering of House Tremere in the west; the East, cut off since Harun's death, plays no part.

diary.title: Tasgillia executed
diary.details: The timeline records the execution of Tasgillia, an event of the Order in the west that the book does not tell.

diary.title: The Fatimids take Egypt, with Berber wizards
diary.details: The Isma'ili Fatimids, caliphs at Qayrawan since 909 on the strength of the mountain Berbers, send their general Jawhar to take Fustat and found Cairo beside it. Berber wizards march with them, working a magic no Muslim mage had met before, and the mages who stand against the invasion are wiped out. No magus of the Order ever meets them, and what their magic was is still unknown.

diary.title: The Schism War
diary.details: From 1003 to 1012 the Schism War tears the Order apart. The Tribunal of the East, still a forgotten backwater, has no recorded part in it.

diary.title: Al-Arama founded
diary.details: Magi raise a covenant on a crag of the Taurus in Lesser Armenia, one of the few founded between the East's first Tribunal and its second, and it grows rich on trade with covenants of the Roman Tribunal.

diary.title: The Holy Lance found at Antioch
diary.details: With the First Crusade trapped inside Antioch, a southern French servant, Peter Bartholomew, tells its leaders that Saint Andrew has shown him in visions where the Lance that pierced Christ lies buried. They dig beneath the cathedral of St Peter, find it, carry it out against the besiegers and break the siege. It is a crusade of portents: comets, saints' ghosts at the head of the armies, visions on every side.

diary.title: The First Crusade takes Jerusalem
diary.details:
On 15 July the crusaders storm Jerusalem and slaughter its people, and Godfrey rules it as Defender of the Holy Sepulchre; a Fatimid army is beaten in August. The sorcerers of Jerusalem had cursed the siege engines and strengthened the walls, but the Muslims' mages are few, scattered and leaderless, and they cannot hold against the Hermetic magi who have come with the armies: Flambeau, Tremere and Tytalus above all, some for their faith, some for plunder, and some Flambeau to avenge a founder they believe Muslim wizards murdered. Arnulf, the new Latin patriarch, finds a relic of the True Cross buried at the Holy Sepulchre.

Secrets
Ever since, the night of 15 July has been a night of the dead in Jerusalem: an Infernal aura of 5 replaces the Divine ones, and the dead of 1099 throng the streets until dawn.

diary.title: Para Belli founded
diary.details: Just after the Crusade, Flambeau magi found a fortress hidden in the Sinai as a refuge for the Order and a school of war for their House's young.

diary.title: The Holy Lance lost; Venti Rosa founded
diary.details: The crusaders carry the Lance into battle until 1101, when it is lost in Asia Minor; what became of it no one knows. The same year Redcaps found Venti Rosa, a covenant that is a caravan, carrying the Order's messages from covenant to covenant across the East.

diary.title: Aedes Veritatis founded
diary.details: Maryam al-Dimashqiyya, a young Jerbiton maga of Damascus, raises a fortress on a mountain five miles east of the city for magi who have chosen to fight their Hermetic brothers on the Muslims' side. She names it the House of Truth; in Arabic, Bayt al-Haqq, it means too the house of what is right.

diary.title: The Levant Tribunal recognised
diary.details: After the Crusade, Verditius magi come for the spoils, Criamon to sit with the East's mystics, Jerbiton for its wealth and learning, and the newcomers stake out covenants and lands over the old covenants' protests. The Grand Tribunal of 1129 recognises the refounded Tribunal and, as the Order now holds covenants across the eastern lands, names it the Levant Tribunal. Recognition brings no order. For decades magi meddle openly in the wars, clash again and again with the Muslims' mages, and fight one another in Wizard Wars over the land's riches; some, sickened by their sodales' cruelty, take the Muslims' side. Crusading magi excuse their breaches of the Code as the price of keeping the Order in the East, counter-crusaders theirs as shielding the Muslims, and the quaesitores, some of them as deep in it as anyone, cannot rule the Tribunal.

diary.title: Edessa falls to Zangi
diary.details: On Christmas Eve Zangi, atabeg of Mosul, takes Edessa and ends the first of the Latin states, with Muslim magi at his side. As Zangi, Nur al-Din and Salah al-Din unite the Muslims, mages gather to their banners.

diary.title: The cursed coins of Damascus
diary.details: The Second Crusade, led by Louis VII and Conrad III, turns on Damascus, Jerusalem's ally, and fails. Some Latins of the Levant sold their comrades for a chest of gold, but the city's sorcerers had enchanted the coins, and when the traitors came to spend them they were brass.

diary.title: The Pyramids (I) founded
diary.details: Ruth of Bonisagus and Pariah of Criamon pitch a camp of tents by the Great Pyramid at Giza. (One of the book's two covenants at the pyramids; see the Pyramids (II), 1178.)

diary.title: Aurora comes to the Levant
diary.details: Aurora Borealis of Jerbiton arrives with Tau of Flambeau and founds Domus Pacis in a khan north of Jerusalem, where magi and the land's other wizards may meet and trade knowledge. In Egypt the Kurd Shirkuh becomes the Fatimid caliph's vizier and dies within the year, and his nephew Salah al-Din takes his place.

diary.title: Nur al-Din dies, or seems to
diary.details:
Nur al-Din, the Muslims' champion in Syria since he took Damascus in 1154, dies, and Salah al-Din begins to bring the Muslim Levant under his own rule. Some say the prophet al-Khidr taught Nur al-Din words of power that won him whatever he asked and carried him great distances in an instant.

Secrets
Khidr may also have taught him long life and foresight: the storyguide may decide he feigned his death, foreseeing Salah al-Din's destiny, and still works unseen for Islam.

diary.title: Heliobus drawn to the temple
diary.details: One of the twelve priests of Thoth and Anubis, hidden in a regio among the pyramids and the Sphinx since ancient times, dies, and as always a Gifted stranger is drawn to take the empty place. This time it is Heliobus Magister, a respected Bonisagus researcher, who arrives as Hermetic magi begin raiding the temple for its magic.

diary.title: The Pyramids (II): the priests join the Order
diary.details: Heliobus brings the priesthood into House Ex Miscellanea and under the Code's protection, and the raids stop. (The book's second covenant at the pyramids; it may stand instead of the first, or beside it.)

diary.title: Aurora goes to Baghdad
diary.details: Seeing the danger Salah al-Din's rise means for the Order, Aurora approaches him, the caliph and their mages, travels to Baghdad to sketch a treaty, and offers it to the quaesitores of Magvillus, who seize on the chance to bring the Tribunal to heel.

diary.title: Hattin
diary.details: Salah al-Din destroys the Latin army at Hattin on 4 July and takes Jerusalem and most of the Latin states. Muslim mages working with him kill many Hermetic magi on the field and later lend magical artillery against the Latin castles, and by the year's end several of the great crusading covenants are gone. The survivors accuse the counter-crusaders of helping the Muslims, but nothing is ever proved. The relic of the True Cross is lost to Salah al-Din on the field.

diary.title: Maryam falls; 'Umar leads Aedes Veritatis
diary.details: Maryam al-Dimashqiyya and most of Aedes Veritatis's magi die at Hattin, though their side has won. Heloise of Criamon, the one left, defers to Maryam's wish, and her young filius Sharaf al-Din 'Umar takes the covenant; Heloise later goes, saying only that it was time, and is not seen again. At Petra the crusaders abandon their castle, leaving Urbs Rubra undisturbed.

diary.title: Foothold founded; Amber joins Aedes Veritatis
diary.details: Two young magi from France, the Flambeau Guillaume de Bourne and the Tytalus Rufus de Clary, plant a covenant on a hill north-east of Acre to keep the Order a lasting foothold on the coast. Amber of Tremere, rejecting her House's support for the Crusades, joins 'Umar at Aedes Veritatis. (By the book's ages Guillaume and Rufus were barely magi; the pack keeps the year.)

diary.title: Richard's truce, and the talks in Baghdad
diary.details: After the Third Crusade retakes Acre and Richard I sells Cyprus to Guy of Lusignan, Richard and Salah al-Din agree on 2 September a three-year truce that leaves the coast to the Latins and Jerusalem to the Muslims. In Baghdad, Aurora's talks between the Order and the Muslims' rulers and mages draw to a close.

diary.title: Salah al-Din dies
diary.details: Salah al-Din dies at Damascus on 4 March, and his sons and brother divide his empire.

diary.title: The Treaty of Baghdad accepted
diary.details: Quaesitores from Magvillus made the Tribunal accept the Treaty Aurora had negotiated, ending the Order's war with the Muslims' mages. Crusading magi could no longer excuse breaches of the Code as defence, nor counter-Crusaders as protecting the Muslims.

diary.title: The Hermetic Embassy founded
diary.details: With the Treaty accepted, Aurora is invited to become a quaesitor, and accepts. She moves to Baghdad to keep the Treaty and founds the Hermetic Embassy there, near the caliph's palace, paid for by Magvillus; soon afterwards she becomes an archmaga.

diary.title: The last Grand Tribunal
diary.details: The Order's most recent Grand Tribunal meets.

diary.title: Esther joins Domus Pacis
diary.details: Esther of Verditius, an Englishwoman, comes to Domus Pacis and soon makes it a channel for trade between the Levant and the Roman Tribunal, breaking al-Arama's hold on the trade.

diary.title: The Treaty renewed
diary.details: The meeting renewed the Treaty for ten years from 1203.

diary.title: The Treaty's second term
diary.details: The renewal voted in 1200 takes effect: the Treaty runs another ten years.

diary.title: Constantinople falls; quarrel with Thebes
diary.details: The Fourth Crusade takes Constantinople on 12 April and founds a Latin empire; few of its knights ever reach the Levant. Greek states rise at Nicaea and Trebizond, Theban magi follow the refugees east, and Thebes claims the border lands for them. War between the two Tribunals is averted by Aurora and quaesitores of both, who give Nicaea to Thebes and Trebizond to the Levant. (The book does not date the settlement.)

diary.title: The Treaty renewed, and a Praeco ruled
diary.details: The meeting renewed the Treaty for ten years from 1213, barely. With Fade and Wraith out of reach, the quaesitores ruled Tau of Flambeau the eldest, and the Tribunal has met at Domus Pacis since.

diary.title: The Treaty's third term; Arash refuses the Oath
diary.details: The renewal won, barely, in 1207 takes effect. At his induction into the Order, Arash, apprentice of Rachel of Criamon, refuses the Oath of Hermes after a crisis of the spirit and swears the Treaty of Barcelona instead. Magi threaten him, and House Criamon spirits him away to Baghdad.

diary.title: A meeting with no renewal
diary.details: The Treaty was not due until 1223, and is renewed only at the last meeting before it lapses, so this meeting had nothing to renew; the debate went on all the same.

diary.title: Felix passes his Gauntlet
diary.details: Felix, born to covenfolk at Domus Pacis, whose Gift showed itself only at twenty-eight while he was a guard there, becomes a magus of Guernicus. His parens Raymond is killed soon after in a fight with a hedge wizard that lames Felix, who takes up Raymond's watch on House Criamon and the Kabbalists. (The book says five years before 1220.)

diary.title: The Fifth Crusade lands in Egypt
diary.details: The crusaders strike at Egypt, the heart of Muslim power, and besiege Damietta. Al-Kamil offers them every old Latin land west of the Jordan and a thirty-year truce if they will leave Egypt, and they refuse. The war strains the Treaty of Baghdad as nothing has since 1193.

diary.title: Damietta falls; the True Cross founded
diary.details: Damietta falls to the Crusade. Two young magi, David of Tremere and Xydas of Bonisagus, found the True Cross in the city, with a few grogs and friends in the garrison, and call on the Order to join them. In Syria al-Mu'azzam pulls down Jerusalem's walls, so that the crusaders cannot hold the city if they take it.

tribunals.secrets:
The book's own guess at what follows 1220: the Treaty fails, perhaps once the True Cross is lost, and the Tribunal joins the war; or it holds until the Mongols come, and then the Mamluks drive the Order from the mainland by 1291, leaving only Cyprus.

The Praeco's office should strictly be Wraith's, of Urbs Rubra, the elder of the Tribunal's two eldest; the quaesitores ruled Tau the eldest in 1207 only because no one could reach her.

neighbours.name: The Order of Suleiman
neighbours.summary:
The Suhhar Sulayman, the great society of sahirs, whom Hermetic magi have long whispered about as a rival Order bent on their ruin. Its members are mostly unGifted Muslim summoners who command jinn and other spirits and work spells and devices much like the Order's; they claim Solomon's powers, taught him (they say) by al-Khidr. About five thousand live east of the Levant, with two or three thousand more in Syria and Egypt, perhaps one in ten of them Gifted; they outnumber the magi about five to one. Founded in 805 by the First Council's heirs, it has a grand vizier elected for life (Kha'trazh, of the Heart, for some thirty years), five Asalat who lead the families, and a vizier for every community of three or more.

The Majlis, its council, meets in Baghdad's summer bazaar for three days each August; only viziers sit, one vote each. Its chief rules: enchanted items go to sahirs only, extracted vis is never sold to magi, a sahir who can be summoned counts as a spirit and may not belong, a sahir silent for five years is lost, and the penalty is expulsion or a fine of vis or service; quarrels go to duels or trials of boasts, stories or champions. When the grand vizier's seat is empty the vizier of Baghdad's Dar al-Hikma acts by custom.

Long turned inward, the Suhhar was shaken by the Crusades. Its sahirs met the invading magi, found most of them proof against Solomonic magic, and lost when they fought them openly; so they worked in secret, guiding rulers, ambushing through the Magic Realm and reading the stars, and helped retake Edessa and break the Second Crusade. By custom a vizier may go in disguise as a nameless sage, 'sending a guide', to offer a promising leader help; Nur al-Din declined, having been taught by al-Khidr himself, and Salah al-Din refused without a word.

In 1220 the Suhhar still counts itself at war with the crusaders and every Hermetic magus among them. It welcomes magi into its lands, where they are easier to watch, studies them closely, and is planning a Solomonic counter-crusade against the Levant. It never signed the Treaty of Baghdad that binds the Levant's magi and the caliph's court, and it treats the Nizaris as traitors.

Its summoning, naranj, Al-Iksir and the rest are the Sahirs tradition's chapter and The Cradle and the Crescent's chapter on the Order.

details.rules: Enchanted items go to sahirs alone; no extracted vis is traded to Hermetic magi; a sahir who can himself be summoned may not be a member.
details.wants: To drive the crusaders, and the magi who came with them, out of the lands of Islam.
details.offers: Solomonic magic, and a guide for a promising ruler or scholar.

neighbours.name: Ashab al-Sakhr, the Followers of the Stone
neighbours.summary:
The family of Solomonic Alchemy, heirs of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the one Gifted member of the First Council. Its seat is Damascus, once the Umayyads' capital and now the heart of the sahirs' war on the invading soldiers and magi. Its members are devout, almost never anything but Muslim, cold to Europeans, proud of their honour, and fond of good steel: many fight with blades rather than spells, or with blades their magic has strengthened. An Asala of the Stone first called the crusaders the Infernal's tools and led the counter-crusade among the Syrian viziers; the family's Asala is usually chosen by a test of arms.

Its house at Damascus is a bayt of the Order of Suleiman, not a Hermetic covenant.

details.wants: War on the crusaders and the magi with them.

neighbours.name: Ashab al-Nahr, the Followers of the River
neighbours.summary:
The family of Solomonic Travel, the art of journeys between worlds: Faerie and the Magic Realm, the Divine and Infernal places, dreams and the land of the dead. It was thought a lesser art until the Nabatean Ibn Wahshiyya, two generations after its founder al-Hajjaj, read its secrets out of the old Egyptians' writings. Its great academy is in Cairo, still the centre of the family's magic. Both founders were known for passion that ended in madness, and the family's sahirs are an eccentric lot.

Its house at Cairo is a bayt of the Order of Suleiman, not a Hermetic covenant.

neighbours.name: The jinn
neighbours.summary:
In Islamic teaching God made three thinking peoples: angels of light, jinn of smokeless fire, and humans of clay. Jinn, like men, can be saved or damned; many have taken Islam, others tempt men and refuse the faith. Iblis was once among the mightiest of them. A jinni's body is Faerie glamour, Infernal power or pure magic, by its realm, usually of Vim and sometimes of an element; most can take a body of matter and change shape.

There are no Divine jinn. The faerie jinn are pious or impious, the magic jinn pagan spirits, genii loci and elementals, the Infernal jinn corrupt. They divide into tribes, said to number 112, which follow their realms loosely: the jann, lesser faerie jinn who keep Islam and pass for merchants, nomads or shepherds; the shaitan, dark faeries and demons; the ghul, faerie predators and Infernal eaters of the dead who haunt graveyards; the marid, ancient spirits of water, wind and weather, mostly in Arabia; and the 'ifrit. Every jinni has a true name, belongs to the lands of Islam, speaks Arabic and knows its theology. The bismillah, the four Quls and the Throne Verse are their weaknesses, and a hajji resists some of their powers.

Many things the common folk call jinn are not: ghosts, naddahas, nisnases, shiqq and the rest, the Persian divs, yazatas and peris, the Soqotran jinniyah, and the planetary spirits the Arabs call al-Nujum, the Stars. Sihr commands true jinn only.

Their lands: Jinnistan, the Mountains of Qaf, Amerabad the City of Amber, Golden Baghdad, Khashgar and the ocean al-Khadar.

neighbours.name: Jinnistan
neighbours.summary:
Wherever jinn make their homes, just out of a man's sight: behind a door that cannot fit between two houses, round the last corner of a bazaar alley, under the ground, in the wilds, in ruins, and beyond this world in regiones and the otherworlds. All of it is Jinnistan. Perhaps it began in the Magic Realm; the tales now put most of it in Arcadia, with branches into Eudokia and perhaps into Hell. Its jinn live much as their human neighbours do and pass freely between the two, and whole jinn cities lie within it, Amerabad the City of Amber among them.

Travellers say it lies past the great rivers, past the eastern mountains, or over the edge of the sea; they are right and wrong at once, for where jinn are, Jinnistan is.

neighbours.name: The Mountains of Qaf
neighbours.summary:
In Muslim lore a ring of peaks around the known world, green as emerald and impassable, the wall between the lands of men and the homes of the jinn and the jinn's homeland. Geographers have put it in the Caucasus, the Pamirs, the Hindu Kush, even the Urals or the Atlas, and the learned match it with the Greeks' great eastern range at the end of Alexander's world.

It may be the very idea of mountains in the Magic Realm, with other worlds behind it, or Faerie's distillation of every tale ever told of mountains no one can cross.

neighbours.name: Iraq
neighbours.summary: The land of the Tigris and Euphrates, settled for thousands of years and in 1220 still thick with towns along the rivers. The faerie gods who once ruled it are seen no more, though their ziggurats still tower over passers-by. Since the 'Abbasids took power in 750 it has been the political heart of Islam, whatever the caliph's real reach; the caliph rules it directly now. North of it lies the Jazira, mostly under quarrelling Ayyubid princes and cities that honour them only in name.

neighbours.name: Baghdad
neighbours.summary:
The caliph's city and so the political centre of Islam, founded by al-Mansur in 762. Its heart is his Round City on the west bank, three walls round the first palace of the Golden Gate; the caliphs spread it over both banks with mosques, palaces and gardens in its golden age. Fire, flood and civil strife have ruined much of it since: on the west bank each quarter stands walled off among ruins, and only the third of the city round the caliph's palace on the east bank thrives. Shi'is and Sunnis, and the Sunni schools of law, quarrel and sometimes fight; the Sufis prosper in the ribats the caliphs build them.

Each summer a vast fair fills the streets and open ground south of the city for most of the season, where anything at all may be bought, from vendors who appear only when their wares are wanted, or whose tents swallow the careless. The Order of Suleiman holds its Majlis there in August. About a thousand sahirs live in the city, more than anywhere else, in eight houses of wisdom, the greatest the Dar al-Hikma north of the palace, with nearly a hundred sahirs and a famous observatory.

neighbours.name: Mosul
neighbours.summary: On the east bank of the Tigris across from the ruins of Nineveh, behind a double wall, a strong citadel and the river; a broad road runs north to south through it and many houses are of marble, with gardens and suburbs outside. Its mosques hold the tombs of Jonah and of St George, a prophet to Muslims too; it has a healing spring, a squash tree the Prophet planted, colleges and Christian monasteries. Its people are Muslims, Christians and Yazidis, and its cloth gives muslin its name.

neighbours.name: Georgia
neighbours.summary: A Christian kingdom of mountains, hills and high plains, with lowland only on the Black Sea coast and along the Rioni and Kura. Its capital Tiflis sits on great trade roads, the Silk Road among them, behind double walls and three strong gates, and for all the wars fought over it is a tolerant city where mosque, church and synagogue may stand side by side.

neighbours.name: Greater Armenia
neighbours.summary:
East of Asia Minor and south-west of Georgia, a war-torn land of mountains, high plains and valleys, with winters of eight months and more. Taken by the Muslims in the seventh century, tributary and free in the ninth, fought over by Muslims and Byzantines (many Armenians left for Lesser Armenia then), and lost to the Turks in the eleventh, it is contested still: the Ayyubids hold some of the south, Trebizond a piece in the north-west, and local dynasties the rest. Greeks, Armenians and Turks grow grain, fish, mine silver and salt, and weave, dye and embroider.

Its remote sites keep strong Magic auras, and its politics leave room for a new covenant that does not grow too strong for its neighbours, if it can be supplied through the winters.

neighbours.name: The Pit of Harut and Marut
neighbours.summary: Beneath the ruins of Babylon hang Harut and Marut, the two angels who taught men magic, chained there for it; some sahirs say they spread the dark, Infernal form of Solomon's art as a test of mankind's faith. The ruins above saw the Tower of Babel, the Jews' exile, Nebuchadnezzar's Hanging Gardens and the Persians' overthrow of Belshazzar. Ancient Magic says more of the city's mysteries.

neighbours.name: Caliph of Baghdad
neighbours.summary:
The 'Abbasid caliph, Commander of the Faithful, al-Nasir, who has reigned since 1180 and is a forceful one. The 'Abbasids have ruled from Baghdad since 762, as figureheads under others for much of three centuries, but since al-Muqtafi (1136 to 1160) the caliphs have governed Iraq themselves, and in 1157 drove the Seljuk sultan from the city. His real realm is little more than Iraq, sometimes the Jazira and parts of Persia too; most Sunni rulers honour him in name, the Ayyubids among them, and he has yet to recognise the Khwarazm-shah's claim to be shah. He has built ribats for the Sufis and restored mosques, shrines and colleges to heal the city's quarrels.

His court is party to the Treaty of Baghdad with the Levant's magi (Blood and Sand). If history holds he reigns until 1225; the Mongols take Baghdad in 1258 and kill the last caliph by rolling him in a carpet and trampling him, so that no royal blood touches the ground.

neighbours.name: Ayyubid Sultan of Egypt
neighbours.summary:
Al-Kamil, sultan in Cairo since 1218, the head of Salah al-Din's family, the Ayyubids, whose princes rule Egypt, Syria, the Jazira and Yemen and spend much of their time plotting against one another. The Hijaz, Mecca and Medina are his in name; his kinsman al-Mas'ud Yusuf holds Yemen and 'Asir more closely.

In 1220 the Fifth Crusade sits in Damietta, taken in 1219 after he offered, and was refused, all the old Latin lands west of the Jordan for the Crusade's leaving Egypt and a thirty-year truce. He camps at al-Mansura. If history holds he reigns until 1238.

neighbours.name: Ayyubid Sultan of Aleppo
neighbours.summary: Al-'Aziz, Salah al-Din's grandson, who has ruled Aleppo since 1216 and holds Edessa, taken from the crusaders by Zangi on Christmas Eve 1144, where most of the people are Christians of several churches. Edessa's Mandylion, the cloth bearing Christ's face, went to Constantinople in the tenth century and was lost in the sack of 1204. If history holds he reigns until 1236.

neighbours.name: Emir of Mosul
neighbours.summary: Mosul has been the Zangids' since 1128; their founder 'Imad al-Din Zangi, who died in 1146, is famed for taking Edessa from the crusaders. In 1220 the real ruler is the mamluk Badr al-Din Lu'lu', regent for the emir al-Qahir Mahmud, who owns the Ayyubids as overlords and the caliph above them, in name.

neighbours.name: King of Georgia
neighbours.summary: Giorgi IV Lasha, king since 1213, of a Christian kingdom free of Muslim rule only since Dawid II took Tiflis in 1121, after centuries of war with Muslim overlords. His people are Georgians, Armenians, Turks, Persians and Alans, Christian and Muslim; the Georgian church answers to neither the pope nor the emperor. His troops prop up the Emperor of Trebizond. If history holds he reigns until 1223.

neighbours.name: Lord of Alamut
neighbours.summary: The dai'd-duat, grand master of the Nizari Isma'ilis, who has held Alamut and its castles in Daylam, Quhistan, Qumis and Fars since 1210. Jalal al-Din Hasan has done what none thought possible and turned the sect Sunni in public; his followers take it for taqiyya and obey, and many think him the imam-qa'im. He looks for friends against the Khwarazm-shah, the caliph in the west and Genghis Khan in the east, has allied with the rulers of Arran and Azarbayjan, and has married the emir of Gilan's four daughters. The Syrian Nizaris at Masyaf answer to him.

neighbours.name: The Nizaris
neighbours.summary:
The Nizari Isma'ilis, whom the crusaders call the Assassins (a slander from Syria; the ascetic Nizaris take no drugs) and the Persians the Batiniyya or the heretics. Their founder Hasan-i Sabbah, a sahir, murdered the Suhhar's grand vizier, fled to Alamut and taught his faith's followers Solomon's art, so that the Nizaris walk unseen, bend minds, poison and cross great distances in an instant. The Suhhar and the Nizaris have tried to destroy each other ever since, with equal losses; the Suhhar still calls them traitors and will not treat with them, while the Nizaris kill sahirs, as anyone else, only when they stand in the imam's way.

Seven ranks: the fida'i and lasiq, uninitiated killers who make the sect's name; the mustajib, the first initiates and its magicians; the da'i, the hujja over each territory or jazira, and the dai'd-duat, grand master of Alamut; and the imam-qa'im, the immortal teacher who was once Elijah, Enoch, Khidr and 'Ali. They seek the hidden meaning of the Qur'an, live by the fifty-one epistles, and hold that the law no longer binds those who know it, so they reject the Pillars and the caliph alike. Members call one another rafiq, comrade.

Besides Daylam, Quhistan and Qumis they keep hidden communities in the southern Zagros (Shardiz among them) and cells in most great cities. The Syrian branch holds Masyaf and a stronghold near Aleppo; its most famous chief, Rashid al-Din Sinan, the crusaders' Old Man of the Mountain, died in 1193.

details.rules: The imam's word is absolute; taqiyya, hiding one's faith, is lawful in danger.

neighbours.name: Sultan of Rum
neighbours.summary:
The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum holds the Anatolian plateau, lost to the empire after Manzikert, and in the north reaches the Black Sea at Sinope, splitting Nicaea from Trebizond. It drove north between them in 1214, killing David Komnenos, but could not reach Trebizond through the mountains. Its sultan Kaykhusraw I died at Antioch-on-the-Maeander in 1211, and the Maeander has been the border with Nicaea since. Trebizond still fears it.

The book names no sultan for 1220. History has Kaykhusraw's son Kaykaus I reign from 1211 to his death about 1220, followed by his brother Kayqubad I, who is named as ruler here.

neighbours.name: Emperor of Trebizond
neighbours.summary:
Alexios Komnenos, thirty-eight, grandson of the Emperor Andronikos Komnenos, who seized Trebizond with his brother David in 1204, the very year Constantinople fell, and calls himself 'Emperor and Autocrat of the Romans'. David pushed west into Paphlagonia and Heraclea, provoking Rum and then Nicaea, which won back most of his gains in 1212; Rum killed him in 1214. Alexios rules on, propped by Georgian troops and Latin and Seljuk mercenaries, cut off from Nicaea and still threatened by Rum, and also rules Cherson and Kerch across the Black Sea; Cherson pays him tribute.

He lives with his family in the castle behind the city. Like his grandfather he patronises art and letters, giving titles and stipends to astronomers, alchemists and experimental philosophers, and his Silk Road market and its taxes make Trebizond very rich.

neighbours.name: The Fifth Crusade
neighbours.summary:
In 1218 the Crusade chose to strike at Egypt, the heart of Muslim power, and laid siege to Damietta. Al-Kamil offered every old Latin land west of the Jordan and a thirty-year truce if it would leave Egypt; it refused, and Damietta fell in 1219. The legate Pelagius claims the conquests for the Church, not the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and the Muslim armies are working their way back toward the city.

Both orders of wizards watch it. Foothold and the Levant's crusading magi want the Treaty of Baghdad voted down in 1221 so they can help it, and the True Cross has opened a covenant in Damietta itself; the Order of Suleiman is planning its own counter-crusade against the Levant.

details.antagonist: The crusaders at Damietta, and the papal legate Pelagius

stages.title: The legate and the king fall out
stages.clues: Pelagius and John of Brienne quarrel over who commands and who keeps what is won.
stages.ignored: John leaves the camp, and the Crusade loses its momentum.

stages.title: The Nile rises
stages.clues: The host marches south toward al-Kamil's camp at al-Mansura.
stages.ignored: The flood cuts the crusaders off; Pelagius agrees an eight-year truce and the Crusade leaves Egypt.

neighbours.name: The Mongol Conquest
neighbours.summary:
As 1220 opens Genghis Khan is camped before Bukhara with a great part of his horde. He has come for the Khwarazm-shah, whose governor at Otrar killed his merchants and who shamed and killed his envoys, and the shah's empire from the Jaxartes to the Gulf is about to fall. The cities the Mongols sack and leave empty may take Infernal auras of wrath, which draw lesser demons, dark faeries, ghuls and evil jinn in the horde's wake, and the unburied dead wander.

If history holds, the Mongols take Persia, Georgia, Armenia, northern Iraq and Asia Minor in the decades after, sack Baghdad in 1258, and are stopped only by Egypt's Mamluks in Syria in 1260. The Levant's magi know almost nothing of them yet.

In Russia and Poland, if history holds, they come twice: a reconnaissance that breaks the princes on the Kalka in 1223, and from 1237 a conquest that burns Ryazan, Vladimir, Chernigov and Kiev, ravages Poland and Hungary, and lays the Mongol yoke on Russia for two centuries. Their spirits run ahead of them: since 1206 wingless thunder wyrms have raided Slavic Arcadia in the Onslaught, and their spies and shamans work among the princes long before the horde returns.

stages.title: Bukhara falls
stages.ignored: The town falls within a fortnight; its defenders are killed, its people enslaved or driven off, and fire leaves it in ruins under an Infernal aura of 3, save round the Kalyan minaret.

stages.title: Samarkand and the Jaxartes towns
stages.ignored: The horde, swelled by Turkish recruits, destroys the oasis towns along the Jaxartes as far as Khojend and takes Samarkand.

stages.title: Gurganj and the shah
stages.ignored: Gurganj falls and its great dykes are broken; the shah is hunted across Khurasan to die on the Caspian shore; Baylaqan in the west is razed.

stages.title: Into Persia
stages.ignored: Balkh, Merv, Nishapur and Herat are sacked, the shah's son is driven over the Indus, and Jebe and Subadei ride north into Russia.

stages.title: The Kalka
stages.clues: Refugee Cumans beg the Russian princes for help; Mongol envoys come with gifts.
stages.ignored: Subadei, having bought off and then destroyed the Cumans, draws the princes' host into a nine-day pursuit and routes it on the Kalka: nine princes die, the Prince of Kiev smothered under a carpet for the murdered envoys. Then the Mongols ride home past the Volga Bulgars, and the Russians forget them.

stages.title: The return
stages.clues: Mongol spies along the steppe; the princes at war over Kiev.
stages.ignored: Great Bulgar is razed; in December the horde enters Ryazan, then burns Vladimir and kills the Grand Prince. Northern Russia submits in four months; Novgorod is spared by the thaw.

stages.title: Kiev falls
stages.ignored: Chernigov and Pereyaslavl are crushed, and on 6 December Kiev is stormed and left a field of bones.

stages.title: Legnica and the Sajo
stages.ignored: Two toumens sack Sandomierz and Krakow and destroy Henry the Pious's army at Legnica; a day later Batu and Subadei annihilate the Hungarian host on the Sajo.

stages.title: The horde turns back
stages.ignored: Word of Ogedei's death recalls Subadei; Batu withdraws to the Volga steppe, razing as he goes, and rules Russia from Sarai.

neighbours.name: The Levant
neighbours.summary:
The lands at the eastern end of the Mediterranean and behind them, as far as the Order's Levant Tribunal reaches: the four Latin states on the coast and Cyprus, Lesser Armenia, Syria, Egypt and Sinai, Asia Minor east of Nicaea, the Alan lands of the Caucasus, Georgia, Greater Armenia and Iraq. Muslims, eastern Christians of a dozen churches, Jews and Latin settlers live side by side, and the Latin states hold only a coastal strip since Salah al-Din's victories.

Faith. Sunni Islam is the faith of the rulers and of most of the people. Its law is taught by four schools, each named for its founder: the Hanafis (Abu Hanifa), the Malikis (Malik ibn Anas), the Shafi'is (al-Shafi'i) and the Hanbalis (Ahmad ibn Hanbal). They read the Qur'an and the hadith a little differently and so part on points of law; the Hanafis, for one, forbid only wine pressed from grapes, and all four argue over beer. The Shi'is of the land and the eastern churches have records of their own.

The Sufis, Islam's mystics, take their name from their plain woollen dress. Their way goes back to al-Junayd and al-Hallaj, whom the authorities put to death for saying he was God made flesh; Ibn 'Arabi is its liveliest thinker now. Lately they have formed brotherhoods, the tariqas, each under a shaykh at a convent or a saint's tomb, and seek God through piety and through dhikr, chanting God's names, and sama', listening to holy music and verse. Once suspected of heresy, they are now thought a force for piety, and rulers build them zawiyas, khanqahs and ribats, which also let them keep an eye on the brotherhoods.

The dhimmis. Christians and Jews, as peoples of a scripture, may live under Muslim rule if they accept the pact of protection: they pay a poll tax, the jizya, rarely more than a dinar a year, may not bear arms, ride horses or build new houses of worship, count for less as witnesses, and sometimes must dress apart. How strictly this is kept varies with the times. The Latin states treat their Muslim, Jewish and eastern Christian subjects in much the same way, and some Latin lords hold them little better than serfs. Hermetic magi stand outside both orders.

Auras. The book's Dominion is the Divine realm, and Islamic, Christian and Jewish auras are all of it: where more than one covers a place, the strongest holds, and the faithful of each religion may draw on the others'. Realms of Power: The Divine's guidance on how strong a Dominion aura is replaces the book's table of Islamic auras by kind of place, which is optional flavour, and the Islamic Temper the book borrows from Pax Dei is simply the Dominion as that book describes it. The book takes all three faiths to be true, as Realms of Power: The Divine does; it names two other ways to play it, none chosen here: God is Law, where Islam alone is right and Christians and Jews must accept Muslim rule to be saved, and God is Love, where Christ's church is right, virtuous Muslims may still be saved, and Muslim auras are weaker or gone.

Foreigners. An optional rule of the book's: in place of the Outsider Flaw for every visitor, a foreigner in the Latin states takes from -5 to +5 on social rolls, as the storyguide judges the state of relations between his people and the land he is in, how much his listener cares, and how plainly foreign he looks. The Definitive Edition's Outsider Flaw still applies to a character who takes it.

The jinn among men. Pious jinn and corrupt ones like to live near people, the first to share in their worship and the second to lead them astray, so they make their homes in regiones at or close to wells, crossroads and rivers; a storyguide may set one at any such place. Heathen jinn keep to the deep wilderness. Their homelands are the Mountains of Qaf and Jinnistan.

Beings named without stats who wander the whole land: Cain, cursed to roam without a home since he killed Abel, his city of Enoch long lost; and perhaps a few of the nephelim, the giant children of fallen angels and mortal women, who destroyed one another at Gabriel's urging, unless some survived, repentant or worse. Rukhkhs with wings thirty paces across, sphinxes, dragons and lesser serpents are in The Medieval Bestiary.

Money. The Latins' gold besant is worth 20 silver deniers, 40 oboles or 240 coppers, and a Mythic Penny is 2 coppers (Acre's record says more). The Muslims strike the gold dinar, the silver dirham and the copper fals; their rates swing, but the book reckons a dinar at 20 dirhams and a dirham at 36 fals. Between the two, a besant passes for a dinar and a denier for a dirham, and a Mythic Penny is worth about 6 fals. Venice, Pisa and Genoa keep communes of their own in the Latin ports, trading under privileges won for their help in the Crusades.

Story seeds:
Unusual Neighbours: in some remote corner jinn and people may still share villages and markets as in Harun's day, and the characters find themselves with very strange neighbours, perhaps easier to live beside than the Latins and Muslims next door.
Braving the Elements: few covenants dare Greater Armenia's eight-month winters, so its magical riches lie waiting; the characters settle there and the weather itself seems to fight them, perhaps by nature, perhaps at the bidding of a powerful magus who resents newcomers.
Seeking Refuge: a badly wounded jinni begs shelter at the covenant and offers his powers in return, not knowing that his enemies, perhaps magi or crusaders, are close behind.
