neighbours.name: The Islamic Tradition
neighbours.summary:
Not a society but a strand running through the Order since its first settlers reached the Levant: magi of any House or faith who have worked Islamic ideas into Hermetic magic to make it more supple, chiefly by using the Islamic ranges, durations and targets. Most are Muslims and most belong to Jerbiton, Criamon or Ex Miscellanea. Its Virtues (Islamic Magic, Interfaith Magic) and Flaws (Poorly-Meshed Hermetic-Islamic Magic, The Faerie Problem) are in the catalog, from Secrets in Sand.

In these times most of its magi keep their heads down, though a few work openly against the Crusade and the crusading magi. Its members are often suspected of counter-crusading, nearly always without cause. A spell may give the Islamic parameters as typed; the book's table matching them to Hermetic ones, and its rule that adapting them for other magi is a major breakthrough, stay in the book.

Story seeds:
A Muslim Hermetic Tradition?: the characters meet a Muslim mage whose magic looks Hermetic and whose line runs back to Harun al-Rashid's court; do they bring him and his fellows into the Order, perhaps as a new House, learn what their magic has become, and face the Crusader magi's anger?

neighbours.name: The Kingdom of Jerusalem
neighbours.summary:
What is left of the Latins' kingdom since Salah al-Din's conquests of 1187: a narrow strip of coast from Beirut in the north down to Ascalon, saved by the crusades of the 1190s. Jerusalem itself is not in it; the capital is Acre. Latin nobles rule over native Christians, Jews and Muslims, who are their subjects. The kingdom lives chiefly on the trade passing from the East to Europe, and grows grain, olives and vines besides. John of Brienne governs it as regent for his daughter Isabel, called Yolanda, and the king of Jerusalem claims precedence over the rulers of Antioch and Tripoli.

The Crusade now in Egypt has opened a quarrel: the papal legate holds that whatever it conquers will not belong to the kingdom, and nothing will settle that until the Crusade is over.

neighbours.name: The County of Tripoli
neighbours.summary: The coast north of Beirut as far as Valania, reaching a little further inland than the kingdom to its south; on its north-eastern side it meets Masyaf and the lands of the Nizaris. Latin lords rule here too, over Muslim, Christian and Jewish natives. When Count Raymond III died in 1187 the county passed to the house of Antioch, so its count is Bohemond IV, prince of Antioch, who counts as the first of his name in Tripoli. Trade brings most of its wealth, with fruit and grain.

neighbours.name: The Principality of Antioch
neighbours.summary: The north-eastern corner of the Levantine coast, much the smallest of the Latin states on the mainland. Bohemond III meant it for his grandson Raymond-Rupen when he died in 1201, but the boy's uncle, Bohemond IV, pushed him aside. Raymond-Rupen won the city back for a while in 1216 and lost it to his uncle again in 1219, the year he also inherited Lesser Armenia from his great-uncle Leon II. He is at Tarsus now making his hold there firm, and is likely to try for Antioch once more when he has; meanwhile Bohemond IV rules from the city.

neighbours.name: Cyprus
neighbours.summary:
The youngest Latin state and the only one off the mainland: an island some 150 miles by 70, with mountains along its north and west and a broad plain over most of the rest. Its fertile land gives most of its wealth, wine and salt above all, and most of its people live in the countryside. Richard the Lionheart sold it to Guy de Lusignan in 1192, and Guy's great-nephew Henry I is king now. The Latins rule but most Cypriots are Greeks, and the island stays Greek in its ways.

The Lusignans brought the mainland's feudal law with them and pressed the Greek majority into subjection, though some wealthier Greeks are still free. Unlike the mainland, the king lets few vassals hold castles, for fear of revolt; the ban on church fiefs is strictly kept; the church is under an archbishop at Nicosia rather than a patriarch; and the king answers to no king of Jerusalem. Its ports are Kyrenia on the north coast, Limassol, once the chief one, and Famagusta, which is taking its trade.

The book suggests that no magus of the Tribunal may yet have settled on Cyprus, which would leave room for a new covenant, if it took care not to alarm the wary Lusignans.

Story seeds:
A Cypriot Covenant?: if no Levantine magi have settled Cyprus yet, its growing trade makes it a fine site for a new covenant, Verditius and Jerbiton magi above all, provided they never alarm the wary Lusignans.

neighbours.name: Lesser Armenia
neighbours.summary:
Cilicia, once the western arm of Greater Armenia: mountains for the most part, with a thin coastal plain that broadens towards the east. A Byzantine land, it filled with Armenians from the east in the tenth century; after Manzikert in 1071 local dynasties set up for themselves, outlasted the Seljuks, and dealt with Latins and Byzantines by turns through the Crusades. Leon II was recognised as king in 1198. He died in 1219 after reigning thirty-two years, and his great-nephew Raymond-Rupen, put out of Antioch, now rules at Tarsus, on an uneasy throne: Tarsus itself would rather have Leon's first cousin Constantine.

It lives on timber from the Taurus forests, goatskins and goat-hair cloth, and is known for its metalwork and its illuminated books; it trades with Genoa and Venice. Its kings keep the Armenian national church, which answers neither to Rome nor to Constantinople. Some Armenian illuminations are said to be enchanted and to glow in the dark, and no one knows who makes them, or why.

Story seeds:
Illuminating Manuscripts: illuminated books from Armenia glow in the dark, and their pictures turn out to be enchanted to some unknown end: the work of a powerful mage, or of an illuminator with the Gift who could be an apprentice?

neighbours.name: Egypt
neighbours.summary:
Muslim since the conquest of 639 to 642, governed for the caliphs until the Fatimids took it in 969; Salah al-Din ended their dynasty in 1171 and brought the land back to Sunni Islam, and it has been the seat of his family's power ever since. His nephew al-Kamil is sultan now. Since the 1160s the Crusaders have known that Egypt is the key to winning back the Levant, and they keep coming: the present Crusade holds Damietta in the Nile delta.

The towns cluster along the Nile, which gives water and carries goods, and the yearly flood keeps the delta and the valley rich; most of the rest is desert, roamed by Bedouin. Egypt trades its own produce and what comes down the Nile or across the Indian Ocean: spices, cloth, grain, sugar and gold. Coptic Christians and Jews live among its Muslims. Its old temples and tombs are everywhere, and priests still call on its ancient gods in their shadow.

Far up the Nile, past Egypt's borders, lies Christian Ethiopia; beyond it, travellers say, the Ring of Fire, where the air is aflame and the sea boils, and past that a land of marvels where Prester John is king.

Story seeds:
Berber Wizards: a new leader rallies the Berber tribes and their wizards, whose unknown magic once won Egypt for the Fatimids, and marches east; if he comes as the Mongols do, the Levant's magi are caught between the two.
Fatimid Survivors?: a Fatimid who escaped Salah al-Din's purge asks the characters to help him back to the caliph's throne, with powerful friends, rich rewards and perhaps an imam's powers, even the right to call the lesser jihad on those who refuse.

neighbours.name: Sinai
neighbours.summary:
The peninsula between Egypt and the Holy Land: mountains in the south ringed by desert, marshes in the north, and fine beaches on the Red Sea shore. All three faiths of the land trace part of their beginnings here, at Mount Sinai deep in the south. Para Belli, the Covenant of Lions, hides a fortress somewhere in its deserts.

Lilith, the first wife of Adam, who left him rather than be ruled by him, made her home by the Red Sea and mothered demons there; she still steals and kills children, boys above all, and Jewish mothers buy amulets from a baal shem against her. She is named here without stats (Kabbalah says more).

neighbours.name: Bilad al-Sham
neighbours.summary:
The country of Syria, as the Muslims call it: the land of the later Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Israel, and the edge of south-eastern Anatolia. Bar what the Latins and a few other Muslim lords hold, Ayyubid emirs govern it under the sultan in Cairo; the greatest of them are al-'Aziz, Salah al-Din's grandson, at Aleppo, and al-Mu'azzam, his nephew, at Damascus.

Two ranges of mountains run side by side from north to south with a rift valley between. A coastal plain, narrow for most of its length, lies between the western range and the sea; the eastern range, lower and more broken, gives way to the Syrian desert, which runs on to the Euphrates. Its valleys are fertile, and the Holy Land is famous for its fruit, sugar cane and indigo and for what it mines and quarries: chalk, marble, sulphur, salt and bitumen. Most of its people are Muslims, with Jews and Christians of many churches among them.

links.note: the ghul who sells his sword to any army

neighbours.name: Asia Minor
neighbours.summary:
The Levant Tribunal's share of Anatolia: everything east of the Empire of Nicaea, which belongs to Thebes by the border ruling. Most of it is the Seljuk sultans' Bilad al-Rum, the Romans' country, theirs since the eleventh century: rugged, crossed by mountain ranges with forests on their flanks, and at its heart a desert plateau between the Pontic mountains to the north and the Taurus to the south. Its towns are many. Turks rule over Georgians, Armenians, Persians and Greeks, most of them Muslim, a hardy people; the townsfolk trade round the Black Sea, with the Russians and the Venetians of Constantinople, through Sinope, and their carved wood and pottery are prized, while country folk raise sheep, goats and very fine fruit.

On the Black Sea coast the Empire of Trebizond is the Levant's too. Two Comnenus brothers, Alexius and David, seized the city from its Byzantine governor within days of Constantinople's fall in 1204 and, with Georgian help, made an empire of the southern shore. Nicaea and the Turks have since cut it back, last when the Turks took Sinope in 1214, and it now owes the Seljuk sultan tribute and soldiers, though it takes tribute of its own from the Crimea. Alexius still reigns. Its mild, fertile coast grows olives and vines among its forests, so it lives by timber, oil and wine, and the Greek church holds sway there.

neighbours.name: The Alan Lands
neighbours.summary: The mountains of the Caucasus and the country north of them, north-east of the Black Sea, where the Alans live in many tribes. Most are Greek Christians, though their loyalty to the church has wavered at times. It is the Tribunal's remotest corner: Urania, its second covenant, has survived here since 806 by being so hard to reach. A people of faeries the magi call the Genjii live near it, so like the jinn that Urania's leader suspects the two share an ancestor.

neighbours.name: The Holy City of Jerusalem
neighbours.summary:
The holiest place in the Levant, sacred to all three of its faiths. For Muslims the Prophet rose from here through the seven heavens on his night journey; Abraham lived here; and here the dead will rise for the Last Judgement. For Christians it is where Christ died and rose again; for Jews, the capital of the Promised Land and the Temple's site. So many holy places make many Dominion auras, and every one of them in the city is a point stronger than it would be anywhere else, up to 10: the city at large has a Divine aura of 4. Where faiths share a site, the strongest aura holds.

The Ghosts of Jerusalem. Ever since the massacre of 15 July 1099 the city has been haunted. Each year on the night of 15 July its Dominion auras give way to Infernal 5, and the ghosts of the slaughtered crowd the streets, shrieking and wailing, until anyone who goes out among them is driven mad; they give back a victim's wits only if they themselves are laid to rest.

neighbours.name: The Dome of the Rock
neighbours.summary: With the Aqsa Mosque, the greatest of Islam's holy places in Jerusalem, raised on the old Temple's ground. Its Dominion aura is 10, and al-Mu'azzam spared the Temple area when he pulled the city down in 1219.

neighbours.name: The Aqsa Mosque
neighbours.summary: The great mosque on the Temple ground, beside the Dome of the Rock; its Dominion aura is 10. The Templars took their name from the part of this enclosure the kings of Jerusalem gave them as their first house, in the order's early days.

neighbours.name: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre
neighbours.summary: The church over Christ's tomb, in all but name the Christians' cathedral of Jerusalem, with a Dominion aura of 10; it was spared when the city was razed in 1219. In 1099 the first Latin patriarch, Arnulf of Chocques, dug a relic of the True Cross out of the ground in its atrium. The Crusaders bore it into battle until Salah al-Din took it at Hattin in 1187, and the Muslims have it still; for a Christian it holds 7 Faith Points.

neighbours.name: The Holy Fire
neighbours.summary: A miracle of every Easter Eve. At noon a holy light breaks out of the tomb itself and climbs into a pillar of flame, the sign of the Resurrection, and a priest lights a candle from it: the Latin patriarch did so while the Latins held the city, and now the senior priest present does. He carries the flame out of the tomb and hands it on through the crowded church while all sing hymns of praise.

neighbours.name: The Western Wall
neighbours.summary: The last of the Temple that stands. Jewish auras have waned everywhere since the Temple fell (Kabbalah says more), but here the Jewish Dominion is as strong as it can be: 10.

neighbours.name: The Hidden Temple of Jerusalem
neighbours.summary:
Jerusalem's Jews whisper that the Romans never destroyed the Temple in 70 AD: God hid it from mortal eyes, and it stands whole in a Divine regio over the city. There it is still in its glory, of limestone and cedar overlaid with gold, with its Holy Place (the hekal) and its Holy of Holies (the debir) among walled courts and outbuildings, and the two great pillars of cast bronze, Jachin and Boaz, still keep the door of its porch.

The Ark of the Covenant once stood in the debir and has been lost since Babylon took the city in 587 BC: hidden, some say, or carried off. It is a chest of acacia wood plated in gold, borne on two gilded poles, with two golden cherubim facing each other on its lid, holding the tablets of the Law, a golden jar of manna and Aaron's rod. It has 7 Faith Points for a Jew and 5 for a Christian. Whether it is in the Hidden Temple the book does not say.

levels.name: The Temple of Solomon
levels.notes: Only the kohanim and rabbis who know the way can reach it. The book gives the regio no aura; 8 is the pack's choice.

neighbours.name: The Horns of Hattin
neighbours.summary: The hill above the Sea of Galilee where Salah al-Din destroyed the Latin army in 1187, took the True Cross and opened the way to Jerusalem. The Order lost as much as the kingdom: Muslim mages killed Hermetic magi in the battle, most of Aedes Veritatis's magi died there with their founder Maryam al-Dimashqiyya, and several Crusader covenants fell with the strongholds they stood by. The book gives it no aura.

neighbours.name: The Great Umayyad Mosque
neighbours.summary:
Damascus's great mosque, built where a church stood until the Muslims took the city in the seventh century and pulled it down. In its ruins, they say, lay the head of John the Baptist, Yahya to the Muslims, skin and hair untouched, and the mosque has kept it since. The head holds 5 Faith Points, for a Christian or a Muslim alike.

Constantinople and several French towns claim the head too. The book leaves the troupe to choose: all but one are fakes; every one is the true head, by a miracle; or there is one head that can be in many places at once, so that what befalls it in one is seen in all. None is chosen here. The book gives the mosque no aura; Divine 6 is the pack's choice.

neighbours.name: The Tower of the Serpents
neighbours.summary:
A tower in Aleppo's walls where a talisman is kept, and while it is there no snake's venom can harm anyone in the city. How its enchantment works is unknown, and so is whether it would work anywhere else. A covenant would covet it, but it would be very hard to steal and harder to keep once word got out. The book gives no aura and no level for the talisman.

Story seeds:
A Tempting Prize: the talisman in Aleppo's Tower of the Serpents keeps every snake's venom from harming anyone in the city; it would grace a covenant, but it is hard to steal and harder to keep once word spreads, and it may not work anywhere else.

neighbours.name: Petra
neighbours.summary:
The old rose-red city in the far south of Bilad al-Sham. A deep, narrow gorge leads in to a meeting of valleys, where caves, chambers and buildings were cut and raised over the centuries, first by the Nabataeans and then by Romans and Byzantines. The Crusaders were the last to build, a castle on a hill deep inside, which they left soon after Hattin. Urbs Rubra, the Tribunal's first covenant, founded in 802, takes its name from the city.

A community of jinn lives in the huge blocks of stone in the entrance gorge. They serve and guard the covenant's two old magi, and have grown so protective of them that they let no visitor through; some of them are strong enough that no Hermetic magus has yet forced a way past. The book gives Petra no aura; Magic 3 is the pack's choice, as for the covenant.

neighbours.name: The Mountains of Northern Syria
neighbours.summary: Wild uplands full of jinn strongholds. The greatest of their jinn is Amirat al-Jabal, the Lady Emir of the Mountain, a marida fifteen feet tall whom a traveller may take for a crag; she cares little for mortals and much for the lesser jinn of the mountains, who look on her as a grandmother (see the Bestiary). The book gives the mountains no aura.

links.note: the marida who watches over the mountains' jinn

neighbours.name: The Mountains of Lebanon
neighbours.summary: The western range above the coast of Tripoli and the kingdom. The Druze, cast out by the Fatimid mission and hunted in Cairo after the caliph al-Hakim vanished in 1021, took refuge in these mountains, where they live still, a secretive people awaiting al-Hakim's return. The book gives the mountains no aura.

neighbours.name: Harran
neighbours.summary: An old city of northern Syria, home to the Sabeans, who keep ancient rites of star-worship; in the first centuries of Islam they were counted among the peoples of the book. The book names them as one of the Levant's many magical traditions without giving them rules, or the city an aura.

neighbours.name: Mount Carmel
neighbours.summary: A mountain of the Holy Land above the coast south of Acre, where a new order of monks, the Carmelites, live on its slopes under a stern rule the Latin patriarch wrote for them: few, but noticed. Hermits seek God in the Levant's wild places too. The book gives the mountain no aura.

neighbours.name: Giza
neighbours.summary:
The plateau on the west bank of the Nile across from Fustat, the greatest of Egypt's ancient monuments. Three great pyramids, between 70 and 160 yards high and sheathed in smooth alabaster, stand in a slanting line from south-west to north-east with lesser pyramids crowded at their feet; some 450 yards to the east a colossal head rises 25 feet out of the sand, the Sphinx, buried to its neck. No one knows who built them or how. Around 820 the caliph al-Ma'mun had the largest broken into: a long passage climbs gently to a burial chamber whose walls are covered with hieroglyphs, and in it his men found only a sarcophagus with some dry bones. Ayyubid sultans have carted off stone from the smaller pyramids, but for all their efforts little of the great ones' casing has come away.

The whole site has a Magic aura of 5, and 6 close by the three great pyramids and the Sphinx. Nobody is sure why. The Bedouin tell of vengeful spirits let loose by al-Ma'mun's workmen and the sultans' quarrymen, stalking the plateau for revenge on those who broke into their tombs. Magi come to it like moths to a lamp, for its secrets and for its aura, which suits laboratory work, though the strength of the aura warps those who stay, and the spirits are not likely to welcome them.

The book offers two covenants here, as alternatives or both at once: the Pyramids (I), two magi in a tent camp by the Great Pyramid, and the Pyramids (II), the priesthood in the regio.

levels.name: The Temple of Thoth and Anubis
levels.notes: A hidden temple near the pyramids and the Sphinx, where twelve priests and priestesses of Thoth and Anubis have kept their gods' worship, little troubled, since ancient times: whenever one died, a new Gifted soul was drawn to the temple to take the empty place. The covenant of the Pyramids (II) if the troupe uses it. The book gives the regio no aura; 6, as by the great pyramids, is the pack's choice.

neighbours.secrets: If the first Pyramids are in play, Ruth and Pariah have mastered the plateau's wandering spirits and use them to learn the pyramids' past and to keep intruders away.

neighbours.name: The Great Pyramids and the Sphinx
neighbours.summary: The ground close about the three great pyramids and the Sphinx, where Giza's Magic aura rises to 6. The hieroglyphs on the walls of the largest pyramid's burial chamber have never been read, and none of the other pyramids has been opened.

neighbours.name: Upper Egypt
neighbours.summary: The Nile valley south of Cairo, upstream, where the naddaha is found most often: an Infernal thing in the shape of an old woman wrapped in a black milaya, haunting wells and oases and calling lone travellers close (see the Bestiary). The book gives the valley no aura.

links.note: the spiked crone who lurks by wells

neighbours.name: Mount Sinai
neighbours.summary: The mountain deep in southern Sinai where God gave Moses the Ten Commandments, holy to Muslims, Christians and Jews alike. At its foot Greek Orthodox monks keep St Catherine's Monastery, which the emperor Justinian founded in the sixth century; the monks trace it back to a little chapel the empress Helena built in the fourth, beside the bush that burned when God spoke to Moses. It bears St Catherine's name because Greek monks found her body nearby some three centuries after she was martyred at Alexandria. The book gives the mountain no aura; Divine 7 is the pack's choice.

neighbours.name: The Taurus Mountains
neighbours.summary: The range that walls the Anatolian plateau off from the south and fills most of Lesser Armenia; its forests give the kingdom its timber. The covenant of al-Arama sits on a crag here, trading with the Roman Tribunal. The book gives the mountains no aura.

neighbours.name: Tarsus
neighbours.summary: The royal city of Lesser Armenia, where Leon II was crowned in the cathedral in 1198 before the papal legate, Conrad of Mainz. Raymond-Rupen has ruled from it since Antioch was taken from him, but its people lean towards Leon's cousin Constantine, and the young king may not keep the throne long. The book gives it no aura.

neighbours.name: Colchis
neighbours.summary:
Western Georgia, in ancient times the rich land of Colchis, where Jason and the Argonauts sailed for the Golden Fleece. What became of the Fleece after Jason died no one knows. The book gives it no aura.

Story seeds:
In Jason's Footsteps: rumour speaks of a new Golden Fleece in western Georgia, old Colchis; the Argonauts' own come home, or some other prize under that name? The way there may hold dangers like Jason's.

neighbours.name: Babel
neighbours.summary:
The ruins of the city where men tried to build a tower to heaven, some fifty miles south of Baghdad, with a faint Magic aura of 1. Under them, sealed by a great mass of rock, is said to be the pit where the fallen angels Harut and Marut hang upside down by their feet, chained by the neck and knees. In creation's first days God judged them lacking in compassion for mankind, gave them human feelings and sent them down to be tempted; both sinned and, offered punishment in this life or the next, chose this one. They taught men magic by God's will, warning each pupil that it was a temptation.

A great rock does lie at the centre of the ruins, thought to stop the pit's mouth; no one alive knows if it does. One man, the tale goes, once got in with a guide and saw the angels hanging there. He had been told never to say God's name in their hearing, but at the sight of them it burst from him, and the angels strained so wildly that their chains almost gave; he and his guide fled and never came back.

neighbours.name: Acre
neighbours.summary:
The capital of the Kingdom of Jerusalem since Jerusalem fell in 1187. The Crusaders took it in 1104 and have held it since, but for the four years Salah al-Din had it, 1187 to 1191. A big, busy port on a sandstone headland, its walls were pushed out to take in the suburb of Montmusard, which grew up outside the old Muslim defences, so a double wall and ditch now cut through the town. Here sit the government, the Latin church (the patriarch of Jerusalem rules from here while the holy city is Muslim) and the military orders, yet Acre's name is bad: courts in the West have begun to punish criminals by shipping them to the Holy Land, and many of them are here. Its Dominion aura hinders magic.

The communes. Settlers who never mixed with the land's people keep apart as nations: Italians, Spaniards and Provençals above all, and the three great Italian cities, Venice, Pisa and Genoa, each as its own. Rewarded with trading rights for their help in the Crusades, they run most of the trade with Europe from quarters in the ports, govern themselves, and answer not to the king but to their home cities, each through an officer in one of the great towns; the Venetians' is a bailli general here in Acre. The law bars commune members from holding fiefs or burgage land, though some have come by them through marriage or sale, and the kingdom's lawyers have never settled what to do about it.

The courts. The Haute Cour judges nobles, and each lord's court his own vassals; in a town the burgesses take their quarrels to the Court of Burgesses, the subject peoples to the Court of the Market (graver cases going up to the burgesses), and anything to do with ships to the Court of the Chain; the communes and the church keep courts of their own. Juries hear most cases, but trial by combat and by ordeal are used at every level.

Money. The Latins strike a gold besant, worth 20 silver deniers, 40 silver oboles (half-deniers) or 240 copper coins; a Mythic Penny is 2 coppers. Byzantine and Muslim coins never went out of use, European money pours in with the trade, and barter is old and common. Minting was the king's alone, but by 1220 some great landholders strike their own coin.

Story seeds:
The Seedier Side of Acre: a thief takes something from the covenant and sells it in Acre, and the characters must follow it from hand to hand through the city's underworld, where the Divine aura hampers their magic and the buyer may open a further story.
neighbours.ruler: John of Brienne, regent for Queen Isabel

neighbours.name: Tripoli
neighbours.summary: Latin since it fell in 1109 and very strong: it stands on a peninsula thrust north-west into the sea, water on three sides and a great wall across the fourth, the south-east. About 4,000 yards that way a castle on a ridge looks down on it, built by Raymond of St Gilles when he first besieged the town in 1102, with gardens and orchards between; off the peninsula's tip lie four islands, a Crusader church on the largest. A busy port, if not Acre's equal, full of Latin and eastern Christians, Muslims and Jews; Genoa, Venice and Pisa all keep communes here, and its cloth and wine are much sought.
neighbours.ruler: Bohemond IV of Antioch, count of Tripoli

neighbours.name: Antioch
neighbours.summary:
On the south bank of the Orontes about twelve miles from the sea, Christian since the Crusaders took it in 1098. St Peter founded his first see here, and a Latin patriarch sits here now. The city fills a plain between the river and Mount Silpius and climbs the mountain's lower slopes, the citadel above it all; its walls carry four hundred towers, so that every stretch is within bowshot of one. Inside are hundreds of houses and markets, and gardens and pasture too; the Onopnicles, a stream of the Orontes, cuts across its north-eastern side. A lively place of trade, home to Latin and eastern Christians. The Holy Lance was found here in 1098, and lost again in 1101.

Story seeds:
Quest for the Lance: signs point the characters to where the Holy Lance, lost in Asia Minor in 1101, now rests; the search may take years and test whether they are worthy of it, within as much as without.

neighbours.name: Nicosia
neighbours.summary: Cyprus's capital, sixteen miles inland from Kyrenia, its nearest port on the north coast, on the Pedheios, a river that runs dry for part of the year but sometimes floods in winter. A round stone wall rings it, and in the middle stands the Latins' great new cathedral of St Sophia, the archbishop's. It is thriving under the Lusignans and fast becoming the finest capital of the Latin states, home to Latins and Greeks.
neighbours.ruler: Henry I of Lusignan, king of Cyprus

neighbours.name: Famagusta
neighbours.summary: A flourishing port on Cyprus's east coast, taking over from Limassol as the island's market because it lies handier for Lesser Armenia and the Latin coast, so merchants abound among its Latins, Greeks and Jews, and foreigners besides.
neighbours.ruler: Henry I of Lusignan, king of Cyprus

neighbours.name: Cairo
neighbours.summary:
Two cities growing into one. 'Amr ibn al-'As, who led the conquest, set his lasting camp of Fustat on the Nile's east bank; the Fatimids founded their new capital, al-Qahira, the Victorious, to its north in 969, and the two together now go by that name. Salah al-Din's citadel was the first great building outside the Fatimid walls, and Giza and Rawda island are favoured places to live. The Ayyubids' chief seat, it is hard to attack and commands the goods moving along the Nile to the coast, so trade and tolls make it rich. It is Egypt's heart in learning and faith as well: Salah al-Din, ending the Fatimid caliphate, founded houses to teach Sunni Islam, and as his first capital it grew a strong class of officials. Christians and Jews live here with the Muslims.

Story seeds:
Under Pressure: al-Kamil's agents ask the characters' help against the crusaders, or against al-Mu'azzam of Damascus; the Code forbids it, the sultan can reward or punish lavishly, and the other side may come asking too.
Recovery Mission: the relic of the True Cross, lost at Hattin, must be won back: the characters must learn where the Ayyubids keep it, perhaps in the sultan's own palace, steal it from its guards and wards, and leave no trace that leads to the Order.

neighbours.name: Alexandria
neighbours.summary: Alexander's city, outshone by Cairo now in Egypt's life but still one of the world's great markets, a match for the Italian cities. Barges bring down the goods of the interior from Cairo; it sells spices, sugar and cotton abroad and buys olive oil, dyes, gems, weapons and the wares of the East. Its yards once built the fleets with which the Muslims took Cyprus. The Pharos, its famous lighthouse, has a mosque in its ground floor and still guides ships with the rest. A great library stood here once, said to have held 500,000 books, which the book has the Romans destroy early in the first century. St Catherine was martyred here.

neighbours.name: Damietta
neighbours.summary:
A city in upheaval. The Crusaders sacked it in 1219 so savagely that Francis of Assisi, who had come with them, judged them more greedy than good and went home to Italy. It is in Latin hands now, its garrison living well and Latin settlers building homes at the expense of the Muslim natives, who bear it more calmly than Latins have borne the same, trusting that all will come right, though they dread another long siege so soon after the last. The Muslim armies, their offer of peace (the True Cross's return among its terms) refused, are slowly fighting their way back towards it.

The sack has left the city's Dominion aura very weak: Divine 1 by day, and nothing at all at night. The young covenant of the True Cross was founded here after the conquest.
neighbours.ruler: The Crusade's leaders (the legate Pelagius claims it)

neighbours.name: Jerusalem
neighbours.summary:
Muslim for four centuries before the Crusade: taken from the Byzantines in 638 and held by Sunni rulers until the Fatimids' reach grew in the tenth century. From 1071 the Fatimids and a Turkish chief, Atsiz ibn Uvak, fought over it for seven years; the Seljuks took it in 1078, the Fatimids took it back some twenty years on, and a year later, in 1099, the Crusaders stormed it. It was Latin until Salah al-Din won it in 1187, and the Ayyubids hold it still.

It is in a sorry state. In 1219 al-Mu'azzam of Damascus, afraid he might have to hand it back to the Crusaders, had it torn down, all but the Temple ground, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the citadel; many houses stand empty, their Muslim owners gone east ahead of the Crusaders they expect. Muslims, Jews and eastern Christians still live here. In peacetime pilgrims of all three faiths come from the West, and the Muslims have never barred them, but with war in the Nile delta and the walls down, few come now.

Story seeds:
The Ghosts of Jerusalem: a character caught out of doors on the night of 15 July, when the dead of 1099 fill the streets, is driven mad, and the ghosts will give back the wits they took only when they are laid to rest.

neighbours.name: Damascus
neighbours.summary:
On the desert's edge at the foot of the Anti-Lebanon, taken from the Byzantines in 635 and the Umayyad caliphs' capital until they fell in 750, when the capital moved to Baghdad and Damascus sank to a province under governors. The Fatimids held it from 970 to 1076, Turkish dynasties after them, and from 1176 Salah al-Din and his heirs; al-Mu'azzam rules it now. It flourished under Nur al-Din and has gone on flourishing: a busy market that even Italian merchants visit in quieter years, famed for silk brocade, copperware, glass and tanned lambskins, with a lively life of scholars and writers, many religious houses founded by the Ayyubids, and able officials. Against the Latins its walls have been made stronger and its citadel rebuilt.

Aedes Veritatis stands on a mountain a few miles east and sells its quarry stone here, which the quaesitores have ruled lawful.

Story seeds:
Scholarly Attention: learned men of Damascus, fascinated by Hermetic magic and its classical roots, court an invitation to the covenant and, once there, will not stop asking questions; the characters must send them home without offending the city's scholars.

neighbours.name: Aleppo
neighbours.summary:
On the little river Quwayq at the north-western tip of the Syrian desert, in the middle of a wide chalk plain. The Muslims took it from the Byzantines in 636 and built a great mosque; for much of the time since it was a frontier town facing Byzantium, fought over often, though mostly governed in the Baghdad caliph's name. 'Imad al-Din Zangi, who would destroy the Latin County of Edessa in 1144, took it in 1128, and under his son Nur al-Din it bloomed with colleges, convents and a hospital. Salah al-Din had it in 1183; his grandson al-'Aziz rules it now.

Salah al-Din's heirs have done well by it: walls repaired, citadel rebuilt, new suburbs for Turkish soldiers, canals mended to reach the whole city, more religious houses, bigger markets, and trade with the Venetians when there is peace. Its farmers grow wheat, cotton, olives, figs, vines and pistachios above all, its herdsmen raise sheep, and it is known for its cloth and soap. In one of its wall towers a talisman keeps the city safe from snakes.

neighbours.name: Konya
neighbours.summary:
The Seljuk sultans' capital since the Crusaders took Nicaea from them in 1097. Once a Byzantine military post that the first Muslim conquests passed by, it fell to the Seljuks in the eleventh century. Unlike the country round it, it is well watered, so it is a centre of farming as well as of rule. It only truly rose after 1118, when Rukn al-Din Mas'ud I raised a mosque there, and more mosques, colleges, markets and walls followed. Greeks, Armenians and Jews live among the Turks, scattered through the town rather than in quarters of their own, and a house's size and height show its owner's rank.

The book has 'Izz al-Din Kay Kawus ruling here; he dies this year, 1220, and his brother 'Ala al-Din Kayqubad succeeds him.

Story seeds:
Preventative Measures: a Criamon seer who has foreseen that the Sufi Jalal al-Din Rumi will settle in Konya in 1226 and found the Mevlevi order sets out to shape it; the quaesitores send the characters, whose covenant lies nearest his road, to stop him before he sets the Order against men and perhaps God.

neighbours.name: The Mountain of Aedes Veritatis
neighbours.summary: A steep peak some five miles east of Damascus, climbed by a single winding track on its western face, crowned by the sandstone fortress of Aedes Veritatis. A quarry near by gives the covenant its stone. The mountain air is clean and keeps those who live there hale. Magic aura 4.
