an airy fire spirit who answers Wardat's summons
a demon Wardat can summon but not command
a jinni bound to Wardat's service
a jinni bound to Wardat's service

neighbours.name: The Khan of Dar al-Salam
neighbours.summary: A roadside inn for merchants under a cliff about eleven miles north of Jerusalem, on one of the quieter trade roads: a walled courtyard ringed by two storeys of rooms, a smithy and stores, with caves hidden beneath it. It is the covenant of Domus Pacis and the meeting place of the Levant Tribunal. Magic aura 1.

neighbours.name: Foothold's Hill
neighbours.summary: A hill about ten miles inland, between Acre to the south-west and Tyre to the north-east. Three of its sides are steep and dangerous; the eastern slope is gentle and wooded, and the covenant has only half-heartedly begun to clear it. Magic aura 2.

neighbours.name: Al-Qurayya
neighbours.summary: A quarter of Baghdad near the caliph's palace, where the Hermetic Embassy keeps its house. The Dominion lies over it at 2, as over most of the city's quarters.

neighbours.name: The Cliffs of Urania
neighbours.summary: Two pale, sun-bleached cliffs meeting deep in the Alan lands north-east of the Black Sea, with a network of caves some fifty feet up where they join: the covenant of Urania. Its remoteness has kept it safe through every war in the region. A people of faeries, the Genjii, live near by; they are much like the jinn. Magic aura 3 (assumed; the book gives none).

neighbours.name: The Fortress of the Lions
neighbours.summary: A fortress hidden in the Sinai desert, the covenant of Para Belli, guarded by two lion statues brought to life by magic. Magic aura 3 (assumed; the book gives none).

neighbours.name: The Crag of al-Arama
neighbours.summary: A mountain crag in the Taurus, in Lesser Armenia, remote and rich in vis, where the covenant of al-Arama stands. Magic aura 3 (assumed; the book gives none).

neighbours.name: King of Jerusalem
neighbours.summary:
Since Hattin the kingdom is a narrow coast running from Beirut down to Ascalon, saved by the crusades of the 1190s and governed from Acre since Jerusalem fell in 1187. Its heir is Isabel, whom many call Yolanda, still a child; her father John of Brienne has ruled for her since 1210 and is king in all but name. Latin lords sit over native Christians, Jews and Muslims, and the realm lives chiefly on the goods that pass through its ports between the East and Europe, with its farms besides.

The crown. A king must be the next heir and be accepted by the barons of the Latin states, though the barons' choice only counts when the succession is disputed. He rules this kingdom and claims a precedence over Antioch and Tripoli. A run of quarrelled-over successions and weak kings, worst after Hattin, let the nobles grow strong at the crown's expense; John has set out to undo that, but he is hampered now, for the legate Pelagius holds that whatever the Crusade wins in Egypt is the Church's and not the kingdom's, and the quarrel waits on the Crusade's end.

The Haute Cour and the offices. The king governs in his High Court with the barons, the masters of the military orders, the heads of the communes and the great churchmen, though the great landholders usually carry it; the same court judges the nobility. The work of government falls to officers chosen from the nobles: the seneschal is the king's deputy, the constable leads his armies, the chamberlain runs his household, and the chancellor, who keeps his letters and his treasury, is always a cleric and of little weight.

Fiefs and burgesses. The kingdom has far more knights than land to give them, so beside the great barons who hold land of the king and enfeoff their own men, many lesser knights hold a money-fief: a fixed yearly sum for their service, some of it barely a living. Such knights depend wholly on their lords and mostly live in the towns. Under the nobles are the burgesses, free commoners sprung from the settlers who came out behind the first crusaders: they hold their houses, gardens and vineyards in burgage tenure for a token rent, work mostly as craftsmen and traders, serve as officials, police, customs men and paid foot, and the most successful have risen in the royal or church service, some even marrying lesser nobles.

The courts. Nobles are judged in the Haute Cour and vassals in their lords' courts; townsmen go to the Court of Burgesses; the subject peoples of a town go to the Court of the Market, which sends grave cases up to the Burgesses; the Court of the Chain hears matters of the sea; and the communes and the Church keep courts of their own. A village wholly of natives follows its own law, but a mixed one is judged by the Latins. Juries hear most cases, yet combat and the ordeal are used at every level. Government writes in Latin, and French is the Latins' commonest tongue.

The subject peoples. Every native, Christian, Jew or Muslim, is a subject of the Latins and ranks below any Latin; the Maronites, united with Rome since 1182, are the exception and are nearly the Latins' equals. Natives may not join a commune and are rarely nobles or merchants; most farm or work a craft, and some serve as dragomans, interpreting between the Latins and the Muslims. Some lords leave their subjects in peace so long as dues are paid, others treat them, Muslims above all, much like serfs, and captives not ransomed are enslaved. Many Latins have learnt to trade and even ally with Muslim neighbours, and zeal for the holy war comes and goes; the new Crusade in Egypt has stirred it up, though not every Latin of the Levant backs it.

If history runs on: Isabel marries the Emperor Frederick II in 1225 and he is king through her; she dies in childbirth, leaving him regent for their infant son. Frederick reaches Acre in 1228 and in February 1229 wins Jerusalem, Bethlehem and a road to the coast by treaty with al-Kamil, the Muslims keeping the Temple enclosure. The city is lost again in 1244, Louis IX of France crusades from 1248 to 1254, and Acre, the last capital, falls to the Mamluks in 1291.
neighbours.ruler: Queen Isabel II (Yolanda); John of Brienne, regent

links.note: Claims the Crusade's conquests for the Church
John of Brienne fights in it

neighbours.name: Count of Tripoli
neighbours.summary:
The county runs north along the coast from about Beirut to Valania and reaches a little further inland than the kingdom; on its north-east it meets Masyaf and the lands of the Syrian Nizaris. When Count Raymond III died in 1187 it passed to the house of Antioch, so its count is the Prince of Antioch, Bohemond, fourth of that name at Antioch and first at Tripoli. Latin lords rule native Christians, Jews and Muslims, and the county lives on trade, fruit and grain.

If history runs on: Bohemond dies in 1233 and his son Bohemond V follows him; Tripoli itself holds out until Qalawun takes it in April 1289.
neighbours.ruler: Bohemond IV of Antioch (Bohemond I of Tripoli)

links.note: Held by the same man, Bohemond IV

neighbours.name: Prince of Antioch
neighbours.summary:
The oldest of the Latin states, on the north-east corner of the coast and much the smallest of them. When Prince Bohemond III died in 1201 the principality should have gone to his grandson Raymond-Rupen, but Raymond-Rupen's uncle Bohemond IV pushed him aside. Raymond-Rupen won it back in 1216 and lost it to his uncle again in 1219, the year he inherited Lesser Armenia; he is now making himself secure at Tarsus and is expected to try for Antioch once more if he can. Bohemond, Count of Tripoli as well, is back in the capital.

If history runs on: Bohemond rules until 1233, and Baybars takes Antioch in May 1268, ending the oldest of the Latin states.

links.note: Held by the same man, Bohemond IV

neighbours.name: King of Cyprus
neighbours.summary:
The youngest Latin state and the only one off the Levantine coast: an island some 150 miles by 70, mountainous in the north and west and a fertile plain elsewhere, living by its farms, with wine and salt above all. Richard the Lionheart took it from Isaac Comnenus on his way to Acre in 1191 and sold it to the Templars, who could not hold it and handed it back; in 1192 he sold it to Guy of Lusignan, whose great-nephew Henry I is king now. The book says no more of him; history has Henry a child crowned in 1218, with his mother Alice of Champagne as regent and Philip of Ibelin as bailli.

The Lusignans have brought the mainland's laws and feudal order to the island, but keep it their own way. The Latins rule a people mostly Greek, mostly rural and Greek in custom, most of them reduced to servitude, though some wealthier Greeks are still free. Fearing rebellion, the king lets few vassals hold a stronghold, and he keeps the Church strictly from holding fiefs. The island's church is under an archbishop at Nicosia, not a patriarch, and its king is a monarch in his own right who owes nothing to the King of Jerusalem. Its ports are Kyrenia, Limassol and, rising fastest, Famagusta. The Lusignans are quick to see a threat to their rule.

If history runs on: Henry reigns until 1253. When the mainland falls in 1291 the military orders withdraw to Cyprus, and it is the one place the Latins, and the Order's magi, stay on: the Lusignans hold it until 1489 and Venice until 1573, when the Ottomans take it.

neighbours.name: King of Lesser Armenia
neighbours.summary:
Cilicia, once a western march of Greater Armenia: mountains with a thin coastal plain that broadens to the east. A Byzantine land, it filled with Armenians fleeing east in the tenth century; after Manzikert in 1071 local dynasties set up on their own, outlasted the Seljuks, and dealt with the Latins and Byzantines by turns as friends and foes, until in 1198 Leon II was crowned king in Tarsus cathedral before the papal legate, Conrad of Mainz.

Leon died in 1219 after thirty-two years, and his great-nephew Raymond-Rupen, put out of Antioch the same year, came to Tarsus to take the crown. His hold is weak: the people of Tarsus would rather have Leon's cousin Constantine, and he may not keep the throne for long. The country lives by timber from the Taurus forests, goatskins and goat-hair cloth, and is famed for its illuminated books and metalwork, which it sells to Genoa and Venice. Its rulers keep the Armenian national church, neither Latin nor Greek.

If history runs on (history, not the book): Constantine's party takes Raymond-Rupen in 1221 and he dies a prisoner the next year; Leon's daughter Isabel is crowned instead, wed first to Philip, a son of Bohemond IV, and in 1226 to Constantine's son Hethum, who reigns until 1270.

links.note: His uncle, who twice put him out of Antioch
His seat, where Constantine is favoured

neighbours.name: The Alans
neighbours.summary:
A people of many tribes in the Caucasus mountains and the country north of them, the far north-eastern edge of the Tribunal. Most are Greek Christians, though their loyalty to that church has wavered over the years; some live in Georgia too. The aloof covenant of Urania lies deep in their lands, kept safe mostly by how remote it is.

If history runs on: Mongol riders under Jebe and Subadei come through the Caucasus in 1222 and beat the Alans, and the Mongols conquer the Alan lands in 1238, destroying Urania with them.

neighbours.name: Ayyubid Sultan of Damascus
neighbours.summary:
Al-Malik al-Mu'azzam 'Isa, nephew of Salah al-Din and younger brother of al-Kamil, who governed Damascus for their father al-'Adil from 1201 and has ruled it in his own right since al-'Adil died in 1218. He holds southern Syria and the Holy Land with Jerusalem, and owns his brother in Cairo as head of the family, though the two are rivals more than allies, as Ayyubid princes tend to be.

In 1219, afraid that the family might have to give Jerusalem back to the crusaders in Egypt, he had the city torn down, its walls first, sparing only the Temple Mount, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the citadel; its Muslims have fled east, leaving whole streets empty. Against the Latins he has made Damascus's walls stronger and rebuilt its citadel, and he and his court favour the city's religious colleges and scholars. Aedes Veritatis, a few miles from his city, sells his builders quarry stone, which the quaesitores have ruled lawful.

How a prince of the Levant rules. The great Muslim houses, the Ayyubids in Syria, the Holy Land and Egypt, the Seljuks in Asia Minor, owe the caliph allegiance and in practice go their own way. The caliph may invest a dynasty's head as sultan, though many take the title unasked. A vizier runs a ruler's civil and military business and can master a weak one. Below him come the emirs, Turks, Kurds, Persians or Arabs, appointed by the ruler, who may give an emir an iqta' (land held for a set number of horsemen, usually hereditary but revocable) or a niyaba (a governorship); the best of both go to the ruler's own kin, and the greatest are styled amir kabir or amir isfahsalar. The ruler names the commanders in war. An army's core is its mamluks, slave soldiers bought young, trained, freed when grown and loyal to their old masters, often Turks, with the emirs' levies, hired men and Bedouin volunteers beside them.

If history runs on: al-Kamil, wanting help against him, sends envoys to Frederick II in 1226; al-Mu'azzam dies in 1227 and his son al-Nasir Dawud follows him, until his uncle al-Ashraf Musa takes Damascus in 1229.

links.note: His brother and rival, head of the family

neighbours.name: Masyaf
neighbours.summary:
The greatest fortress of the Syrian Nizaris, in the hills where the County of Tripoli ends on the north-east, and the seat of their chief. The sect took it with the other Syrian castles as its power spread in the twelfth century. Salah al-Din laid siege to it in 1176 and gave up, the tale goes, after he woke to find a poisoned dagger and a threat from Rashid al-Din Sinan in his tent; another story has Sinan's envoy show the sultan that his own two bodyguards would kill him on Sinan's word. After that Salah al-Din kept on good terms with Sinan. The book gives the castle no aura: a Muslim castle-town's Divine 2 is assumed.

If history runs on: Baybars takes the last Syrian Nizari fortresses in 1273.

neighbours.name: The Syrian Nizaris
neighbours.summary:
The Syrian branch of the Nizari Isma'ilis, the Assassins of the crusaders' tales, holding Masyaf and a chain of castles in the hills between the County of Tripoli and the Orontes. The name comes from hashishi, a slur their enemies used. The sect began with Hasan-i Sabbah, who seized Alamut in Persia in 1090 and backed Nizar, the Fatimid heir set aside in 1094; Nizar died in prison at Alexandria, but the Nizaris hold that a grandson was smuggled to Alamut and reared there, and Alamut's masters have claimed the imamate since 1162. The sect is ranked strictly under its head at Alamut; its religious leaders are called shaykh, or pir in Persian, and members call one another rafiq.

Most of what is told of them comes from their enemies: that boys were raised to blind devotion, drugged and woken in a garden made to look like Paradise, then sent out with a dagger and the promise of going back. Their greatest Syrian chief, Rashid al-Din Sinan, the crusaders' Old Man of the Mountain, ruled from 1162 until about 1193 and was said to be a magician.

The Assassin's dagger. A Syrian Nizari is armed with a gold-hilted, bright-bladed dagger which, when drawn, gives the man it was made for, and no other, the effect of Endurance of the Berserkers (ReCo 15 in the Definitive Edition), three times a day. Alamut's masters, who are chosen by birth and are not always magicians, cannot always make them, so the Syrian chiefs send batches east from time to time.

If history runs on: the Mongols destroy the Persian strongholds in 1256, and Baybars takes the last Syrian ones in 1273.

Story seeds:
Stolen Property: the characters chance on a shipment of Assassins' daggers bound from Syria to Persia and only learn what they are in the lab; the Nizaris want them back, and others, the Order among them, want them too.

details.rules: The chief at Masyaf obeys the master at Alamut, and every rafiq obeys his chief.
details.wants: Their castles kept, and any ruler who threatens them cowed
details.offers: A killing, a warning, or a ruler's ear

neighbours.secrets:
In this saga the chief of the Syrian Nizaris is always a magician. Blood and Sand makes him usually a raqi and sometimes a sahir or another tradition's man; The Cradle and the Crescent's Nizari mustajibs, renegade sahirs, are the faction's tradition here. He breeds his followers' fanatical loyalty with tricks and spells together.

A shipment of daggers bound for Alamut is a prize many would want, the Order among them, and the sect will hunt down whoever holds one.

neighbours.name: The Old Man of the Mountain
neighbours.summary: The da'i who leads the Syrian Nizaris from Masyaf, whom the crusaders call by the name they gave Sinan, the Old Man of the Mountain. He answers to the master at Alamut, Jalal al-Din Hasan, though Syria is far away and its chiefs have often gone their own way. The book does not name the chief of 1220.

neighbours.name: The Bedouin
neighbours.summary: The Arab nomads of the deserts, in Syria, Sinai, Egypt and the steppe toward Iraq. Some tribes have emirs and settled lands, but many still wander as they please, outside the settled order. They trouble the rulers of the towns now and then, but mostly keep on good terms with them and send volunteers to their armies. Many are Twelver Shi'is, and spirit masters are common among their tribes. Bedouin by Giza tell of vengeful spirits in the pyramids.

details.wants: Their grazing, their wells and their freedom
details.offers: Guides across the desert, and riders in war

neighbours.name: The Turcomans
neighbours.summary: The Turkish nomads who came west off the Asian steppe, grazing their herds across Asia Minor, the Jazira and the edges of Syria. Like the Bedouin, some follow emirs and have settled, while many more wander outside any ruler's order, an occasional menace to the towns and a ready source of horsemen in war.

details.wants: Pasture, plunder and their own chiefs
details.offers: Horse archers for any prince who pays

neighbours.name: The Knights Templar
neighbours.summary:
The Order of the Temple, the first of the military orders: a few knights who banded together about 1118 to guard the pilgrim roads to Jerusalem, were given part of the Temple enclosure by the king and the patriarch, and took their name from it. Their life as warrior-monks was set down about 1128 and made a Rule in 1129, and their task soon grew from the roads to the defence of the whole Latin East. Since Jerusalem fell their headquarters has been Acre; they hold Tortosa and are building the Pilgrims' Castle at 'Atlit. Grand Master Peter de Montaigu leads them; his brother Guerin leads the Hospitallers.

The military orders. Brotherhoods of warrior-monks, sworn to poverty, chastity and obedience and to their order's Rule, who answer in matters of religion only to the Pope, which sets them at odds with the local clergy. Popes have heaped privileges on them, lords in Europe have given them land to pay for the war, and in the East the crown and nobles, short of men and money, have handed them castle after castle. Their wealth has paid for houses that recruit for them, their brethren are the core of every Latin army, their masters are men of state, and the Templars and Hospitallers now bank for the kings of Jerusalem. They are not the king's vassals and owe him only the loyalty of the Latin states' defenders, which does not always mean following his policy.

In play: a knight brother takes the Definitive Edition's Brother Knight, a sergeant Brother Sergeant, a priest Brother Chaplain; Templars wear a red cross on white, Hospitallers a white cross on black, Teutonic Knights a black cross on white, and the lesser orders their own marks. The book's Turcopole, a light horseman of an order, is nearest Brother Sergeant.

If history runs on: the three great orders withdraw to Cyprus when the Latin states fall in 1291 and are blamed for the loss. Philip IV of France has the Templars of France arrested in October 1307 for heresy, obscene rites and idol worship; many confess under torture, the Pope takes over the inquiry, fifty-four are burnt at Paris in 1310, the order is suppressed in 1312 and much of its land goes to the Hospitallers, and in March 1314 Grand Master Jacques de Molay and Geoffroi de Charney are burnt.
neighbours.secrets:
Whether the Templars were guilty is not known, and the book offers a troupe the darker reading: Templars who really are diabolists or sorcerers with real power. With their houses and wealth across Europe and the Levant they would be a rival to the Order itself, and if their power is Infernal, Hermetic magic cannot see through the deceptions that hide it, so only mundane digging will find them out.

Story seeds:
Templar Sorcerers?: the troupe may make the Templars sorcerers or diabolists with real power, a rival to the Order across Europe and the Levant; if their strength is Infernal, Hermetic magic cannot see it, and companions and grogs must trace it by mundane means.

neighbours.name: The Knights Hospitaller
neighbours.summary:
The Knights of St John, brothers of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem: a brotherhood founded in the tenth century to run a hospital for the sick of Jerusalem, which took up arms in the twelfth and by its middle was the second military order of the Latin East. Its headquarters was in Jerusalem, and is now at Acre; Krak des Chevaliers and Marqab are its great castles. Grand Master Guerin de Montaigu leads it.

If history runs on: it outlives the Templars, takes Rhodes from the Byzantines in 1310 and crusades from the island into the sixteenth century.

neighbours.name: The Teutonic Knights
neighbours.summary:
The Order of St Mary of the Teutons, the youngest of the three great orders. It traces itself to a German hospice in Jerusalem of the early 1100s, lost when the city fell in 1187, and to a field hospital German crusaders made at Acre from their ships' sails and timbers in the Third Crusade, which Clement III approved in 1191 and Celestine III privileged in 1196; it became a military order the next year, and Innocent III confirmed it in 1199. It has grown fast, with houses across Europe and its heart in Germany, whence its interest in the Slav lands; it will never be a great force in the Levant. Grand Master Hermann von Salza leads it from Acre.

If history runs on: it moves its headquarters to Marienburg in Prussia in 1309 and turns to eastern Europe.

neighbours.name: The Order of the Trinity
neighbours.summary: One of the lesser military orders of the Latin East, founded in the twelfth century or later. The book names it among them and says no more.

neighbours.name: The Order of the Sword
neighbours.summary: One of the lesser military orders of the Latin East, founded in the twelfth century or later. The book names it among them and says no more.

neighbours.name: The Order of the Holy Spirit
neighbours.summary: One of the lesser military orders of the Latin East, founded in the twelfth century or later. The book names it among them and says no more.

neighbours.name: The Order of St Lawrence
neighbours.summary: One of the lesser military orders of the Latin East, founded in the twelfth century or later. The book names it among them and says no more.

neighbours.name: The Order of St Thomas of Acre
neighbours.summary: Its house is at Acre. One of the lesser military orders of the Latin East, founded in the twelfth century or later. The book names it among them and says no more.

neighbours.name: The Order of St Lazarus
neighbours.summary: The Order of Leper Knights: monks who kept a leper hospital in Jerusalem early in the twelfth century and had become a military order by its middle, now at Acre. It is said that its master and its knights must all be lepers themselves.

neighbours.name: Chastel Pèlerin
neighbours.summary:
The Pilgrims' Castle at 'Atlit, on a headland south of Haifa, which the Templars began building in 1218 with crusaders' help and are still raising: a sea-girt fortress meant to replace the castles lost after Hattin. The book does not name it; it is history's.

The book gives it no aura; a castle of an order of monks, with its chapel, is taken as Divine 3.

neighbours.name: Tortosa
neighbours.summary:
The Templars' coastal stronghold in the County of Tripoli, with its keep by the sea and its old cathedral of Our Lady. The book does not name it; it is history's.

The book gives it no aura; a castle of an order of monks, with its chapel, is taken as Divine 3.

neighbours.name: Krak des Chevaliers
neighbours.summary:
The Hospitallers' great castle on its ridge above the gap between Tripoli and Homs, held since 1142 and the strongest in the Latin East. The book does not name it; it is history's.

The book gives it no aura; a castle of an order of monks, with its chapel, is taken as Divine 3.

neighbours.name: Marqab
neighbours.summary:
The Hospitallers' black basalt castle above the coast road near Valania, theirs since 1186; the book has it the last of their great strongholds to fall, to Qalawun in May 1285.

The book gives it no aura; a castle of an order of monks, with its chapel, is taken as Divine 3.

neighbours.name: Montfort
neighbours.summary:
A hill castle in Galilee, north-east of Acre, which the Teutonic Knights buy in 1220 to make their own seat. The book does not name it; it is history's.

The book gives it no aura; a castle of an order of monks, with its chapel, is taken as Divine 3.

neighbours.name: The Papal Legate
neighbours.summary:
Pelagius, cardinal bishop of Albano, the Pope's legate with the Fifth Crusade, who leads it from Damietta. He holds that every land the Crusade wins in Egypt belongs to the Church, not to the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and he and John of Brienne quarrel over that and over who commands. He refused al-Kamil's offer of all the old Latin lands west of the Jordan, with the True Cross given back, for the Crusade's leaving Egypt.

The True Cross. The fragment Arnulf of Chocques, the first Latin patriarch, found buried in the Holy Sepulchre's atrium in 1099 went into battle with the crusaders until Salah al-Din took it at Hattin in 1187; it has been in Muslim hands ever since, perhaps in the Ayyubid sultan's palace in Egypt. For a Christian it is a relic of 7 Faith Points; for anyone else it is wood.

If history runs on: the quarrel stalls the Crusade in 1220; in 1221 the Nile flood traps the host outside al-Kamil's camp at al-Mansura, and Pelagius buys its way out of Egypt with an eight-year truce.

links.note: Leads it as the Pope's legate

neighbours.name: The Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem
neighbours.summary:
The head of the Latin Church in the Kingdom of Jerusalem, over its archbishops and bishops, who has sat at Acre since the Muslims retook the Holy City. The book names no patriarch; history has Ralph of Merencourt. With the Patriarch of Antioch he heads the Latin Church on the coast. Early on the clergy tried to master the kings and failed; now the crown mostly controls the clergy, the king choosing the patriarch and bishops of his realm. The Church may not hold fiefs, yet it has been given much property, and from that it owes the royal host its contingents.

Most monks in the Levant, nearly all of them in houses founded since the crusaders came, are Benedictines; there are hermits besides, and pilgrims, Christian and Jewish, still go up to Jerusalem each year, as the Muslims allow. Before the Latins lost the city the patriarch lit the Holy Fire on Easter Eve; the senior priest present does it now. The True Cross, the kingdom's holiest relic, lost at Hattin, is in the legate's summary.

neighbours.name: The Latin Patriarch of Antioch
neighbours.summary: The head of the Latin Church in the Principality of Antioch and the County of Tripoli, in the city where St Peter founded his first see. The book names no patriarch; history has Rainier, from 1219.

neighbours.name: The Latin Archbishop of Nicosia
neighbours.summary: The head of the Latin Church on Cyprus, an archbishop and not a patriarch, at the royal capital, where the Latins have raised the great cathedral of St Sophia in the city's heart. The king strictly keeps the Church from holding fiefs. The book names no archbishop; history has Eustorge of Montaigu, from 1217.

neighbours.name: The Carmelites of Mount Carmel
neighbours.summary: A new order of hermits, few but notable, living on the slopes of Mount Carmel by a hard rule the Latin Patriarch wrote for them (history names him Albert, about 1209).

neighbours.name: St Catherine's Monastery
neighbours.summary: At the foot of Mount Sinai, a house of Greek Orthodox monks founded by the Emperor Justinian in the sixth century; the monks trace it back to a little chapel the Empress Helena built in the fourth beside the burning bush from which God spoke to Moses. It is named for St Catherine, martyred at Alexandria, whose body Greek monks found close by some three centuries after her death.

neighbours.name: The Melkite Church
neighbours.summary:
The Greek Orthodox of the Levant, called Melkites, who kept communion with Constantinople when the Council of Chalcedon in 451 defined Christ as one Person in two natures, human and divine. They stood first among Christians while the Byzantines ruled; the Latins have pushed their clergy aside and held them down hard, but they are still found everywhere in the Levant. The book names none of their patriarchs.

The native Christians under Latin rule are subject peoples, ranked below every Latin (the Maronites alone excepted); under Muslim rule they are dhimmis.

neighbours.name: The Jacobite Church
neighbours.summary:
The Syrian Orthodox, named for their founder Jacob Baradaeus: Monophysites, who rejected Chalcedon and hold that Christ has a single nature, most often both human and divine. They live mostly in Syria and the Holy Land. The book names none of their patriarchs.

The native Christians under Latin rule are subject peoples, ranked below every Latin (the Maronites alone excepted); under Muslim rule they are dhimmis.

neighbours.name: The Coptic Church
neighbours.summary:
The greatest church of Egypt, Monophysite like the Jacobites, and since rejecting Chalcedon ever more cut off from the rest of Christendom. Its patriarch of Alexandria sits at Cairo; history has the see empty from 1216 to 1235, which the book does not mention.

The native Christians under Latin rule are subject peoples, ranked below every Latin (the Maronites alone excepted); under Muslim rule they are dhimmis.

neighbours.name: The Ethiopian Church
neighbours.summary:
The church of the Christian kingdom of Ethiopia, founded in the fourth century and Monophysite, cut off from other Christians since the Muslims took Egypt. Some Ethiopians still come north on pilgrimage to Jerusalem and the holy places, and a few of its monks keep a house there; its head is in Ethiopia. Beyond Ethiopia, travellers say, lies the Ring of Fire, where the air burns and the sea boils, and past it a land of wonders under the good Christian king Prester John.

The native Christians under Latin rule are subject peoples, ranked below every Latin (the Maronites alone excepted); under Muslim rule they are dhimmis.

neighbours.name: The Armenian Church
neighbours.summary:
The national church of both Armenias, Christian since the fourth century, which rejected Chalcedon and went its own way. It is said to be Monophysite but has never joined the other Monophysite churches in full communion. In Lesser Armenia it is the rulers' faith; in Greater Armenia the rulers are Muslims. The book names neither its catholicos nor his seat.

The native Christians under Latin rule are subject peoples, ranked below every Latin (the Maronites alone excepted); under Muslim rule they are dhimmis.

neighbours.name: The Georgian Church
neighbours.summary:
The national church of Georgia, Christian since the fourth century: once under the patriarch of Antioch, it has governed itself since the eighth, and answers to neither Pope nor Emperor. The book names none of its heads.

The native Christians under Latin rule are subject peoples, ranked below every Latin (the Maronites alone excepted); under Muslim rule they are dhimmis.

neighbours.name: The Maronite Church
neighbours.summary:
The Syrian Christians of the Lebanon who would not accept the Council of Constantinople's ruling of 681 that Christ has two wills, divine and human, and kept apart until they united with the Latin Church in 1182. They take their name from Maro, a saint of the fifth century. Since the union they have nearly the Latins' standing in the Latin states, and a Maronite is made as a Latin character, though usually with Arabic as his first tongue and without the subject peoples' lower status. The book names none of their patriarchs.

The native Christians under Latin rule are subject peoples, ranked below every Latin (the Maronites alone excepted); under Muslim rule they are dhimmis.

neighbours.name: The Church of the East
neighbours.summary:
The Nestorians, strongest in Iraq and Persia: outside the Roman and Byzantine empires, they had no part in the great councils and are of two minds about Chalcedon, since they understand Christ's Person differently, stressing his true humanity and the reality of his moral choices. Its catholicos sits at Baghdad. The book names none of its heads.

The native Christians under Latin rule are subject peoples, ranked below every Latin (the Maronites alone excepted); under Muslim rule they are dhimmis.

neighbours.name: The Rabbinites
neighbours.summary: The Jews who follow the rabbis and the Talmud, the larger of the Levant's two Jewish communities, found in every town of note and a subject people under Latin and Muslim rulers alike. Kabbalah (Fourth Edition) says more of them; Jewish characters may use its guidelines.

neighbours.name: The Karaites
neighbours.summary: The Jews who hold to Scripture alone and reject the rabbis' oral law, the second of the Levant's two Jewish communities. Kabbalah (Fourth Edition) says more of them; their magi are Realms of Power: The Divine's Karaites.

neighbours.name: The Druze
neighbours.summary:
Isma'ili extremists who took the sixth Fatimid caliph, al-Hakim (996 to 1021), whom others thought mad, for a manifestation of God, led by Hamza ibn 'Ali. When al-Hakim vanished in 1021 Hamza said he had withdrawn to test the faithful; Hamza vanished soon after, and al-Muqtana led them. Their scripture, the Rasa'il al-Hikma, the Epistles of Wisdom, is Hamza's and al-Muqtana's letters, and they await the return of both. The Fatimids disowned them and hunted them in Cairo, but survivors fled to the Lebanon mountains, where they live still, so secretive that little more is known of their faith. Their name comes from al-Darazi, another of the sect's early men.

The Fatimids were the other branch of the Isma'ilis: they held that each prophet's outward teaching hides one inner truth, a God past knowing from whom the world came by emanation; their rulers claimed to be both imams and caliphs but left the people Sunni. They ruled Egypt from 969 until Salah al-Din ended them in 1171. Some say a Fatimid escaped him.

details.rules: Their doctrine is kept secret from outsiders.

neighbours.name: The Nusayris
neighbours.summary: A splinter of the Twelvers, also called 'Alawis for their devotion to 'Ali, whose teaching the rest of the Twelvers rejected. They date from 859 and Muhammad ibn Nusayr al-Numayri, who called himself the bab, the gate, to the imam. They teach that a spirit stands just below the ineffable God, whose emanations reach down rank by rank into the world to lead fallen souls out of their bodies to heaven, and read the Qur'an as an initiation into devotion to 'Ali. They live in the Bahra' mountains of northern Syria.

neighbours.name: The Twelvers
neighbours.summary:
The Ithna'ashari or Imami Shi'a, the largest Shi'i branch, many of the Bedouin among them. They follow twelve imams from 'Ali down through his house. The eleventh, al-Hasan al-'Askari, died in 874, and his son Muhammad al-Mahdi went into the lesser occultation, speaking through four envoys in turn, until the last of them said on his deathbed in 941 that the imam had entered the greater occultation, to last until he comes back as the mahdi at the end of time. Until then he is with his people but silent, and several duties, the lesser jihad among them, are suspended.

Shi'i law. The Shi'is differ from the Sunnis mostly in putting the imams' teaching, handed down by their jurists, first: they allow temporary marriage and have their own rules of divorce and inheritance, and for most of them the lesser jihad waits on the rightful imam, now hidden. Five Shi'i branches matter in the Levant: the Twelvers, the Nusayris, the Fatimid Isma'ilis, the Druze and the Nizaris; the Qarmatians, the other early Isma'ili movement, were revolutionaries of Kufa.

neighbours.name: The Renewal of the Treaty of Baghdad
neighbours.summary:
Muslim law lets a truce stand for ten years at most, so the Treaty of Baghdad must be renewed every decade. It was renewed for 1203 and, by a whisker, for 1213; the meeting at Domus Pacis in 1221 must decide whether it runs again from 1223. The Crusade in Egypt has put it under more strain than ever. Foothold, Para Belli and the True Cross want it thrown out so that they can help their kin at Damietta; Aedes Veritatis backs it, since it shields the Muslims; the Hermetic Embassy and Domus Pacis argue that without it the Tribunal falls back into the chaos before 1193.

Both sides are already counting heads. The aloof covenants have not made up their minds, and Heliobus of the Pyramids speaks for twelve magi. The Praeco and the presiding quaesitor do not vote. If the Treaty is kept little changes; if it falls, the Embassy must leave Baghdad at once, and Foothold is likely to be the first covenant to burn.

details.antagonist: The Crusader covenants, led by Foothold

stages.title: The scramble for votes
stages.clues: Rufus de Clary speaks for Foothold in every covenant that will hear him; envoys from the Embassy and Domus Pacis follow on his heels. Redcaps of Venti Rosa carry letters, promises and threats. Each side asks what Heliobus wants, and how the covenants of Urania and al-Arama, far from the war, mean to vote.
stages.ignored: The Crusaders arrive with their votes in hand and the mediators with hopes.
stages.stopped: The undecided covenants are won for renewal before the meeting.
stages.turned: The troupe becomes the broker both sides must court, and names its price.

stages.title: The meeting at Domus Pacis
stages.clues: Tents rise outside the khan and the gate shuts on all but magi. Scipio takes the chair; the motion to renew is heard, the speakers chosen, and Foothold's charge against 'Umar may be brought the same week to cost the counter-Crusaders their leader.
stages.ignored: The vote goes the way the Crusade's news from Egypt blows that season.
stages.stopped: The Treaty is renewed for ten years from 1223. Give the ruling a term ending at the meeting of 1228, the last before the next lapse.
stages.turned: The renewal passes with terms the troupe wrote, or the Treaty is remade to bind more than the Order.

stages.title: The Treaty lapses
stages.clues: Without a renewal the Treaty ends with its term. Crusader magi ride for Egypt; Aedes Veritatis's allies come into the open; the caliph's mages and the Ayyubids' prepare for war.
stages.ignored: The Tribunal slides back into open war with the Muslims' mages and with itself; the Embassy flees Baghdad and the quaesitores lose their grip.
stages.stopped: A new treaty is patched together before the fighting spreads.
stages.turned: The troupe treats with the caliph's court on its own account, and becomes the Order's new voice there.

neighbours.secrets: The book's guess at the future: the Treaty fails, perhaps once the True Cross is lost at Damietta, and the Tribunal joins the war; or it holds until the Mongols, after which the Mamluks drive the Order off the mainland. If it is broken, the Crusader magi may plan a strike at the caliph's mages in Baghdad (see the Hermetic Embassy's story seeds), and openly pro-Muslim covenants such as Aedes Veritatis are the first to be Renounced.

neighbours.name: The Secret War on Foothold
neighbours.summary:
Foothold, two quarrelsome French magi on a hill above Acre, leads the Crusader covenants and calls loudest for war; the quaesitores mark it as a danger to the peace and suspect it of crusading still, though nothing has been proved. Aedes Veritatis, the counter-Crusaders' fortress outside Damascus, is its declared enemy, and the two trouble the Embassy with politics at every turn.

Foothold's magi care more for conquest than for their own house: its woods are half cleared, its labs poorly kept, and its French grogs have begun to grumble. It may take a sharp blow to wake them.

stages.title: Mishaps at Foothold
stages.clues: Foothold's fishing boats are lost, its merchant robbed, its grogs fall out among themselves; things said in its hall are known in Damascus within days.
stages.ignored: Foothold weakens without knowing why.
stages.stopped: Foothold's magi find the scrying devices and see the hand behind their troubles.
stages.turned: The troupe learns who is spying on whom, and can sell or keep the knowledge.

stages.title: The grogs on the edge
stages.clues: Open mutterings among Foothold's men-at-arms; a stranger among them who stirs every quarrel; Guillaume trains harder and listens less.
stages.ignored: The turb rises against its masters.
stages.stopped: Guillaume and Rufus deal with the trouble in time.
stages.turned: The troupe wins the turb's trust, and a door into Foothold.

stages.title: A blow in the night
stages.clues: Foothold is struck directly by unseen hands: walls breached, a lab burned, a magus nearly killed. Rufus carries the outrage to the quaesitores and names Aedes Veritatis.
stages.ignored: Foothold and its allies answer in kind, and the Treaty's enemies point to the war as proof it is dead.
stages.stopped: The quaesitores trace the attack, and Aedes Veritatis's magi face charges.
stages.turned: The troupe proves who struck, or hides it, and both covenants owe it a debt.

stages.title: Open war
stages.clues: The secret war breaks into the open, or the Treaty lapses and there is no longer any need for secrecy.
stages.ignored: Foothold falls, the first casualty of the new war, or Aedes Veritatis is Renounced and besieged.
stages.stopped: The quaesitores impose a peace on both covenants.
stages.turned: The troupe ends the feud on terms both sides can stomach, and earns both their thanks and their suspicion.

neighbours.secrets: Since 1193 'Umar, his sodales and their allies, Hermetic and mundane, have waged a hidden war on the Crusader covenants, Foothold above all, and the quaesitores have not caught them. Aedes Veritatis has spies in Domus Pacis who learn everything said there, and Foothold has its own there who hear what is said in council. Mages in the Ayyubids' service have hidden scrying devices in Foothold to warn of any attack.

neighbours.name: 'Umar's Double Loyalty
neighbours.summary: Sharaf al-Din 'Umar, a Jerbiton elementalist and devout Sunni, has led Aedes Veritatis since Hattin, a careful leader now though the counter-Crusade still rules him. To the people of Damascus his fortress is the home of a reclusive emir, a part he plays when he must. Foothold has learnt that early in his career he killed a Crusader magus who attacked him, with no one to witness that it was self-defence, and means to see him Renounced.

details.antagonist: The sultans' claim on 'Umar, and Foothold's hunt for it

stages.title: Errands for the sultan
stages.clues: 'Umar is away when no one expects it; Ayyubid officers in Damascus treat the 'emir' with odd respect; news of crusader plans reaches the sultans' courts uncommonly fast.
stages.ignored: His service runs deeper with every season.
stages.stopped: 'Umar keeps the two loyalties apart, for now.
stages.turned: The troupe learns the secret, and holds it over him or keeps it for him.

stages.title: A shadow from the past
stages.clues: Foothold asks the troupe to help bring 'Umar before the quaesitores for the old killing, perhaps on the word of the dead magus's ghost.
stages.ignored: The charge reaches the meeting of 1221.
stages.stopped: The charge fails for want of a witness.
stages.turned: The troupe finds the truth of the fight, and with it a hold over Foothold or over 'Umar.

stages.title: Discovery
stages.clues: A quaesitor, Felix perhaps, or Scipio, comes upon proof that 'Umar serves the Ayyubids. Amber and Wardat learn it with everyone else.
stages.ignored: The quaesitores move to Renounce him.
stages.stopped: The proof is lost or never believed.
stages.turned: The troupe persuades 'Umar to give up one master before the Order chooses for him.

stages.title: Renounced
stages.clues: 'Umar is Renounced and flees to the Muslims' mages, who take him in; Aedes Veritatis must choose between its leader and the Order.
stages.ignored: The counter-Crusaders lose their head and the Order gains a powerful enemy who knows its secrets.
stages.stopped: He is taken before he reaches his allies.
stages.turned: 'Umar becomes the troupe's link to the Muslims' mages, an outlaw and a go-between at once.

links.note: A quaesitor who may find out
One of the sultans he serves

neighbours.secrets: 'Umar is sworn to the Ayyubid sultans as well as to the Order, and serves them in secret; not even his own sodales know. If the Order finds out he will almost certainly be Renounced, but he is powerful and would call on the Muslims' own mages to shelter him, so a Renunciation need not mean his death.

neighbours.name: Esther's Trade
neighbours.summary: Esther of Verditius, an Englishwoman at Domus Pacis since 1197, has made the covenant a channel for goods between the Levant and the Roman Tribunal and its trade its chief income. In doing so she broke al-Arama's long hold on that trade, and its magi curse her name and would help anyone against her if they thought they could get away with it. She is not above a little mind magic to win a bargain.

stages.title: A shipment to Rome
stages.clues: Esther offers the troupe a handsome fee to carry a sealed shipment from Domus Pacis to a covenant of the Roman Tribunal, and will not say what is in it.
stages.ignored: Her trade grows, and with it her risks.
stages.stopped: The troupe refuses, and she finds other carriers.
stages.turned: The troupe learns what she trades, and to whom.

stages.title: Devices in the wrong hands
stages.clues: An emir's guard turns a blade that should have cut him; a Latin lord's tower is warded against fire. Al-Arama's magi start asking where such things come from.
stages.ignored: Al-Arama gathers its evidence.
stages.stopped: The devices are recovered quietly.
stages.turned: The troupe takes over the trade, or uses the proof to bind Esther to it.

stages.title: The charge
stages.clues: Al-Arama lays the evidence before the quaesitores. Felix, under the same roof, must investigate his own sodalis; the Praeco's covenant is shamed.
stages.ignored: Esther is convicted, Domus Pacis loses its income and its standing as a neutral house, and the mediators lose votes.
stages.stopped: The charge cannot be made to stick.
stages.turned: The troupe brokers a settlement that gives al-Arama back part of the trade.

neighbours.secrets: She grows rich on her own account by selling potent enchanted devices to Muslim and Latin nobles, which the Peripheral Code forbids as meddling. If the quaesitores learn of it, her sodales at Domus Pacis, the Praeco and a quaesitor among them, will suffer with her. She also draws Terram vis from a source of her own that no one else knows.

neighbours.name: Rufus's Hoard
neighbours.summary: Rufus de Clary of Tytalus speaks for Foothold at the Tribunal. Handsome, cunning and ready to spend others to get his way, he can work magic without words or gestures and read the lips of people across a room, and he has learnt a great many things other magi would rather keep hidden. Several of them fear what happens if he ever gets proof. In debate he says the Crusade must go on for the Order's good.

stages.title: Sins of the father
stages.clues: A character's parens comes asking for help: Rufus has proof of something that could see the parens executed under the Code, and has begun to hint at a price.
stages.ignored: The parens pays, and Rufus gains a servant.
stages.stopped: The proof is stolen or destroyed.
stages.turned: The troupe finds where Rufus keeps his proofs, and who else is in them.

stages.title: Votes for silence
stages.clues: Magi who owe Rufus their silence begin to speak against the Treaty, or stay away from the meeting of 1221.
stages.ignored: Blackmail tips the renewal vote.
stages.stopped: His victims band together against him.
stages.turned: The troupe frees his victims, who owe it instead.

stages.title: The diabolist's son
stages.clues: Someone digs into Rufus's childhood, or a demon that knew his parents comes looking for him.
stages.ignored: His past comes out, and the Order wonders whether the son learnt his parents' trade.
stages.stopped: Rufus buries the past again, at a price.
stages.turned: The troupe holds Rufus's own secret, and with it Foothold's voice.

neighbours.secrets: Rufus's zeal is fear, not faith. His parents were diabolists who tormented him as a child until his master Gilles de Clary rescued him, and he believes demons still hunt his soul. He gathers magical power, and means to take his share of the East's riches when the Order conquers it, to protect himself. His own past is the one secret he would kill to keep.

neighbours.name: Amber against Her House
neighbours.summary:
Amber the Golden of Tremere, gold of skin, hair and eye since a laboratory accident in her apprenticeship, joined Aedes Veritatis in 1188 because she would not accept her House's support for the Crusades. That put her in disgrace with her House's elders, and only her parens Catullus, a senior magus of Coeris who treats her as his protegée, has kept her from being disciplined.

Catullus is drifting towards Final Twilight, and Amber will soon need other friends. She is fiercely independent, and her bond with her cat familiar Luigi is the only tie she has ever welcomed.

stages.title: Catullus fades
stages.clues: Letters from Coeris grow vague and then stop; Catullus still holds Amber's sigil, and Tremere magi in the Levant ask after her loyalties.
stages.ignored: Amber's protector is gone before she has another.
stages.stopped: Catullus's last act secures her standing.
stages.turned: The troupe becomes the ally Amber needs, at a time she can repay it.

stages.title: The House remembers
stages.clues: Tremere magi of the Levant, the young David at Damietta among them, are told to bring Amber to heel; she is summoned to answer for her defiance.
stages.ignored: She is ordered to leave Aedes Veritatis.
stages.stopped: Her House is persuaded to let her be.
stages.turned: The troupe argues her case within the House's own customs.

stages.title: Discipline
stages.clues: The House moves against Amber, through its own law or through the Tribunal, and 'Umar must decide whether to stand by his friend.
stages.ignored: Amber is broken or driven out, and the counter-Crusaders lose a maga.
stages.stopped: Amber defies them and keeps her place.
stages.turned: Amber leaves House Tremere, and the troupe helps her find a new House or a new covenant.

neighbours.name: Aurora's Twilight
neighbours.summary: Archmaga Aurora Borealis of Jerbiton, quaesitor and maker of the Treaty, is 102 and failing. A severe Twilight not long ago damaged her command of Animal, and she can feel her hold on the world loosening. She fears for the Levant if she goes soon, for the Embassy's only other magus, Spiral of Criamon, is enthusiastic, wise in the Sufis' eyes and almost impossible to understand, and no diplomat. She is looking hard for an answer.

details.antagonist: Time, and the Twilight that is claiming Aurora

stages.title: Storm clouds
stages.clues: Aurora is absent from her duties for days at a time; servants speak of her talking with no one; she flinches at every thunderstorm.
stages.ignored: Her work falls more and more to Spiral.
stages.stopped: Her Twilight is slowed, perhaps by rare lore or a Criamon's help.
stages.turned: The troupe earns her trust as she weighs who should follow her.

stages.title: The search for a successor
stages.clues: Aurora sounds out magi who might keep the Treaty after her; Magvillus sends its own candidates; Foothold and Aedes Veritatis each want a friendly face in Baghdad.
stages.ignored: No successor is ready.
stages.stopped: A trusted diplomat joins the Embassy in time.
stages.turned: A player magus is chosen.

stages.title: The second bolt
stages.clues: Lightning strikes Aurora and she passes into Final Twilight, or very nearly.
stages.ignored: Spiral is left to deal with the caliph's court alone, the Treaty loses its architect, and the border with Thebes loses its guarantor.
stages.stopped: Her successor takes over without a gap.
stages.turned: The troupe keeps the caliph's trust through the change, and the Treaty's future rests on it.

neighbours.secrets:
When she was eight, lightning struck Aurora, wakening her Gift, and showed her how she would end: a second bolt carrying her into Final Twilight.

If the Embassy is still in Baghdad when the Mongols take the city in 1258 it falls with it, and Aurora, old and weak, is taken by the Mongol shamans (see her story seeds).

neighbours.name: Fade and Wraith
neighbours.summary: Fade and Wraith of Criamon, husband and wife at Urbs Rubra in Petra, are the Tribunal's eldest magi, so by right Wraith should be Praeco. A people of jinn living in great stone blocks in the gorge before the covenant serve and guard them, and have grown so protective that they let no visitor through; some are too powerful for any magus to pass. No one has seen the pair for years, and in 1207 the quaesitores gave up and ruled Tau the eldest. Most magi think the jinn killed them long ago and keep up the pretence for reasons of their own.

stages.title: Who is Praeco?
stages.clues: Someone at the Tribunal, for a motive of their own, argues that Tau's office belongs to Wraith if she lives, and that someone should find out.
stages.ignored: The question lingers over every ruling Tau makes.
stages.stopped: The Tribunal confirms the ruling of 1207.
stages.turned: The troupe is sent to Petra to learn the truth.

stages.title: The gorge
stages.clues: The jinn of the stone blocks bar the way, with bargains, illusions and, if pressed, force.
stages.ignored: Visitors are turned back, or not seen again.
stages.stopped: The jinn are persuaded or bested.
stages.turned: The troupe wins the jinn's trust by showing it means their masters no harm.

stages.title: The Red City's heirs
stages.clues: Fade and Wraith are found, or their bodies are. Either way the oldest covenant of the Tribunal, its lore and its jinn want new masters.
stages.ignored: The jinn keep Urbs Rubra for themselves, and its secrets with it.
stages.stopped: The pair are left in peace and the Praeco's office settled.
stages.turned: The troupe becomes Urbs Rubra's heirs, or Wraith, lucid for a day, claims the Praeco's chair.

neighbours.secrets: They live: senile, close to Final Twilight and heedless of the Tribunal's business, while the jinn shut out a world their masters can no longer face.

neighbours.name: Heliobus's Bloc
neighbours.summary: Heliobus Magister of Bonisagus was drawn to the hidden temple of Thoth and Anubis at Giza in 1177, when one of its twelve priests died, and brought the priesthood into House Ex Miscellanea. Since then he has seemed to care only for studying the rites of his fellow priests. But with one vote to each magus he commands twelve at the Tribunal, and the more political covenants are uneasy at what he could do with them, and at what powerful magic the temple may keep.

details.antagonist: Heliobus Magister and his twelve votes

stages.title: Courted
stages.clues: Envoys of the Crusaders and of the mediators find their way to Giza with gifts; Heliobus receives them politely and promises nothing.
stages.ignored: He keeps his own counsel until the vote.
stages.stopped: He promises to stay away from the meeting.
stages.turned: The troupe learns what he really wants.

stages.title: The price
stages.clues: Heliobus names a price for his votes: lore, vis, a ruling in the priests' favour, or the troupe's help with something hidden in the temple.
stages.ignored: The side that pays most gets the bloc.
stages.stopped: Neither side will pay, and he abstains.
stages.turned: The troupe pays, and buys a friend.

stages.title: A power at the Tribunal
stages.clues: Heliobus finds he enjoys being the kingmaker, and brings motions of his own.
stages.ignored: Every meeting turns on Giza's twelve votes, and covenants begin to question whether the priests are true magi at all.
stages.stopped: A challenge to the priests' membership checks him, at the cost of bitterness.
stages.turned: The troupe and Heliobus lead the Tribunal together.

neighbours.name: The Theban Border
neighbours.summary: After 1204 Theban magi fled east with the Greek refugees and their Tribunal claimed more of Asia Minor for them; Aurora and quaesitores of both Tribunals settled it, Nicaea going to Thebes and Trebizond to the Levant. Thebes says its magi, driven out by the Latins, deserve more room; the Levant says the Thebans' failure to defend themselves and the Latins' doings are no affair of its. Both have agreed to differ, and it would take very little to set them at each other's throats.

details.antagonist: The Theban magi who want more of Asia Minor

stages.title: Newcomers
stages.clues: A Theban magus settles in Trebizond's lands, harvests vis there, or claims a site a Levantine covenant had marked.
stages.ignored: Others follow.
stages.stopped: The newcomer is warned back over the border.
stages.turned: The troupe makes the newcomer a friend.

stages.title: Words at the border
stages.clues: Grogs come to blows over a vis source; each Tribunal sends a Redcap with a protest; Aurora is too ill to ride north.
stages.ignored: Wizard War is declared across the border.
stages.stopped: Quaesitores of both Tribunals meet and calm it.
stages.turned: The troupe settles the dispute and becomes the border's go-between.

stages.title: Two Tribunals at odds
stages.clues: Each Tribunal votes to defend its claim; the matter is talked of for the next Grand Tribunal.
stages.ignored: The Levant fights a second war on its northern border while the Crusade burns in the south.
stages.stopped: A new settlement is agreed and sworn.
stages.turned: The border is redrawn in the Levant's favour, or the troupe's.

neighbours.name: Arash and the Oath
neighbours.summary: Arash, once apprenticed to Rachel of Criamon, refused the Oath of Hermes at his induction in 1213 and swore the Treaty of Barcelona instead, the peace between the Order and the Kabbalists. Magi threatened him, and House Criamon carried him off to Baghdad, where he studies the Kabbalah with the city's rabbis and struggles to make his Hermetic and Kabbalistic gifts agree. A Gifted man trained in the Arts who is outside the Order troubles magi who read the Code strictly.

details.antagonist: Magi who would treat Arash as an unsworn wizard

stages.title: Found
stages.clues: Word reaches the Tribunal that Rachel's lost apprentice lives in Baghdad's Jewish quarter, close to the Embassy. Felix of Guernicus, who watches Criamon's dealings with the Kabbalists, is asked what he knows.
stages.ignored: The rumour spreads among the Crusader magi.
stages.stopped: House Criamon quietly moves him again.
stages.turned: The troupe reaches him first.

stages.title: Join or die
stages.clues: Magi who threatened him in 1213 come to Baghdad, and the rabbis who teach him close ranks. The Treaty of Barcelona and the Embassy's peace are both in the way.
stages.ignored: Arash is killed or driven out, and the Kabbalists ask whether the Order keeps its treaties.
stages.stopped: The quaesitores rule that his oath under the Treaty of Barcelona protects him.
stages.turned: Arash finds a way to reconcile his two magics, and the troupe gains his friendship and his insight.

neighbours.name: The True Cross's Call
neighbours.summary: Two young magi, David of Tremere and Xydas of Bonisagus, founded the True Cross in Damietta after the city fell to the crusaders in 1219. With a small turb and friends in the garrison they are stripping a Muslim sorcerer's estate of its magical relics and making the port a channel for the East's treasures to the magi of Europe. They have called on the Order for magi to join them, but few will come until Damietta is safer.

details.antagonist: The Muslim armies closing on Damietta

stages.title: The call
stages.clues: A Redcap brings David's letter: magi wanted at Damietta, rich pickings promised, the dead sorcerer's house half searched.
stages.ignored: No one answers, and the two stay alone.
stages.stopped: The covenant is persuaded to leave while it can.
stages.turned: The troupe answers, and has the first choice of the sorcerer's treasures.

stages.title: The sorcerer's estate
stages.clues: Something in the estate does not want to be carried off, and the Muslim mages who knew its master want it back.
stages.ignored: The relics, and their curses, reach Europe.
stages.stopped: The dangerous pieces are sealed away.
stages.turned: The troupe returns them, and wins Muslim friends.

stages.title: Damietta falls again
stages.clues: The Crusade founders in the Nile flood, the truce gives Damietta back, and the True Cross must flee or be taken with the city.
stages.ignored: The covenant is destroyed with its magi, and the Crusaders cry for vengeance.
stages.stopped: The magi escape with what they can carry.
stages.turned: The troupe gets them out quietly, before anyone blames the Order or the Muslims.

neighbours.secrets: If history runs its course the crusaders lose Damietta in 1221, and the book suggests the loss of the True Cross may be what finally breaks the Treaty.

neighbours.name: The Opening of the Pyramids
neighbours.summary: At Giza, Ruth of Bonisagus and Pariah of Criamon live only for the pyramids. They have bent the wandering spirits of the place to their will, set them to teach the monuments' history and to keep strangers off, and are working to read the hieroglyphs in the burial chamber of the greatest pyramid and to find a way into the others, hoping for the ancients' hidden wisdom and a way past the limits of Hermetic magic. Other magi find their single-mindedness disturbing; nobody knows how far they will go.

stages.title: Restless spirits
stages.clues: Travellers near the pyramids are driven off by terrors; local guides refuse to go near; the two magi buy every Egyptian text they can find.
stages.ignored: The work goes on unwatched.
stages.stopped: Others persuade them to go carefully.
stages.turned: The troupe joins the work, and shares the finds.

stages.clues: Ruth and Pariah decipher enough of the burial chamber's writing to learn how a sealed pyramid might be opened, and what was shut inside.

characters.summary:
Scipio of Guernicus, filius Rognvald, the Tribunal's senior quaesitor and so the chair of its meetings, which gives him great power. He keeps no covenant and spends his time travelling the Tribunal. Ninety-six, he looks to be in his sixties: strongly built, with short grey hair and a beard, always in robes of grey. A master of Intellego, above all Intellego Mentem, he knows most of the common Intellego spells of the other Forms too.

The book leaves his character to the troupe, as three readings, none chosen here: a rigid Traditionalist who enforces the Code to the letter; a Transitionalist who lets reason come before law; or a corrupt judge in some covenant's pay.

characters.summary:
Head of Aedes Veritatis, filius of its founder Maryam al-Dimashqiyya. Hattin was a Muslim victory, but it killed most of the covenant's magi; the one left, Heloise of Criamon, honoured Maryam's wish and let the young 'Umar take charge, and later went her own way, saying only that her time had come, and has not been seen since. Wild and hot-headed once, he has grown into a careful, wise leader, though the counter-Crusade still obsesses him and the old wildness breaks out now and then.

To look at he is nobody special, neither tall nor short, black-haired and fully bearded, until he speaks: then people listen. He wears black robes with a white sash and a white turban, and never goes without his staff, enchanted to carry him from place to place in an instant and to turn weapons aside. Like his mater he is an elementalist and a devout Sunni, and of the Islamic Tradition. His elements have made other Arts hard for him, Vim most of all: the second time he renewed his longevity potion he could make it strong enough only with rare ingredients, and hunting such things has become his own quest.

Story seeds:

characters.secrets: 'Umar is a servant of the Ayyubid sultans as well as a magus of the Order, and not even his sodales know it. If the Order learnt of it he would probably be Renounced; but he is powerful and would call on the Muslims' own mages for help, so a Renunciation might not end in his death.

characters.summary:
Amber of Tremere, filia Catullus, came to Aedes Veritatis in 1188, soon after Hattin and the Muslims' retaking of Jerusalem, because she would not bow to her House's backing of the Crusades. She is now the covenant's second magus and 'Umar's close friend. Fiercely independent, she is tied all the same to 'Umar, to her cat familiar Luigi, and to her parens Catullus of Coeris, who treats her as his protégée and has so far kept the House's elders from disciplining her. Catullus is drifting toward Final Twilight, and she will soon need other friends in the House.

A mistake with two reagents during her apprenticeship blew up in her face, threw her into Twilight for a while and left her skin, hair and eyes the colour of gold; the bond with Luigi has slit her pupils like a cat's. She is short and lithe, catlike in her manner, with a gift for magic touching felines. She wears a loose red robe that comes off easily, for she often changes shape, into a cat or a leopard, by spells she made herself. Luigi is a cat of ordinary size whose white fur ends in gold; he picked her as much as she picked him.

description.biography:
A sahira of the Hermetic Sahirs, the House Ex Miscellanea tradition of Houses of Hermes: Societates, whose package (Sihr, a Minor Magical Focus in jinn, Twilight Prone) she takes in place of the Fourth Edition's sahir rules; that tradition is Iberian and rare in the Levant, so she is an outlier. She keeps no Arts and no Parma Magica, as printed (ArM4's sahirs could not learn Parma; HoH:S's have Arts). Her Sihr is 6 on the Art table: modest. ArM4 gave every sahir Magic Sensitivity and Second Sight, which are on her sheet.
Her Familiarities, the old rules' knowledge of particular beings that eased their summoning: 'Aziza 3 (her grandmother's ghost), Hiss 2 (an airy fire spirit), Lucius 3 (a demon, whom she may call but never command), al-Manqa'i 3 and Sharif 3 (jinn of the Ghul and Marid tribes, her bound jinn), and the planets Mars (al-Mirrikh) 3, Jupiter (al-Mushtari) 4 and the Sun (al-Shams) 4. Her planetary invocations stretch a spell's Range, Duration or Target as vis once could for a magus: a power of the sahirs that Hermetic magic no longer has, kept as story.
The jinni al-Abyad, the White, has plagued her since she was a child; finding how to beat him is her life's work, and she leaves her rooms only when the fight against the Crusaders needs her. Her sigil is a copper bracelet; a faint smell of roses rises as she works.

characters.summary:
The Rose of Jerusalem, a sahira, the youngest magus of Aedes Veritatis and one of the few of the land's own sahirs to join the Order. A staunch Sunni sworn to the counter-Crusade, she joined only to be protected from the Crusader magi, with 'Umar as her sponsor. Her magic is Sihr: she summons and bargains with spirits, ghosts, jinn and a demon, and calls on the planets.

Tall and strongly made, she goes wrapped in a black milaya that shows only her sharp face and her bare feet; her black eyes hold whoever meets them, and spirits trail after her awaiting her orders. She knows she frightens people and uses it, with her power over minds, to be left alone at her studies. When she chooses to talk she is lucid and good company, which is seldom. Since childhood the jinni al-Abyad, the White, has tormented her; she spends her time looking for a way to beat him, and comes out of her rooms only when she is needed against the Crusaders. A faint smell of roses marks her magic.

characters.summary:
Tau of Flambeau, filius Sigma, leader of Domus Pacis and Praeco of the Tribunal since 1207, when the quaesitores ruled him its eldest. At 133 he still seems a Flambeau of the usual kind, loving fire, too sure of himself and boyish; under the roguish manner he is a kind and honest man who wants to do right by people, cleverer and of wider magical interests than his House's type, though few look past the surface.

His master Sigma, a wandering Flambeau, passed into Final Twilight just before Tau's Gauntlet, on the road to a covenant in Scotland. Tau went on alone to the House of Hermes' Wisdom, whose head soon sent him to find the nearest gathering of his House for his Gauntlet. A magus at last, he lived a long while among the magi of a Greater Alps covenant, until a younger sodalis there, Aurora of Jerbiton, made plans for a covenant in the Levant; he came with her and helped her found Domus Pacis, content to stay in the background, and took it over at her urging when she left for the Embassy.

Once a dashing young man, he is slower now and very hard of hearing, and looks to be in his seventies: silver curls to his collar, a goatee, laughing eyes and a friendly smile. He dresses well, in a leather tunic, breeches and polished black boots, with a shortsword at his side.

Felix of Guernicus, filius Raymond, a quaesitor. He was born at Dar al-Salam to one of the covenfolk and was a guard in its turb when his Gift showed itself at 28; after the usual fifteen years of apprenticeship he passed his Gauntlet only five years ago. Soon after, his parens was killed fighting a hedge wizard, in a skirmish that crippled Felix's right leg for good. He took over Raymond's standing duty of watching the dealings between House Criamon and the Levant's Kabbalists, and does it faithfully, by ordinary means first, since he knows his magic is weak and best kept in support. He is on good terms with the Kabbalists and has quickly won a name for fairness in the Order.

He wears plain brown robes and walks with a staff; he can fight but seldom goes armed, as his leg makes it hard and battle no longer stirs him.

characters.summary:
Esther of Verditius, filia Enrico Bellini, the newest magus at Dar al-Salam, who joined in 1197 and has fast become its most valued. Her passion is the Levant's trade: through her merchant contacts she has made herself and the covenant rich, and under her the covenant is a channel for goods between the East and Europe, above all between the Levant and the Roman Tribunal. Her trade is now its main income. It has also made bitter enemies of the magi of al-Arama, whose monopoly she broke.

An attractive woman of middle height and build, with short fair hair, pale skin and an unmistakably English accent. She wears simple white robes under a blue hooded cloak she has enchanted with several powers, a plain gold circlet, and tools and casting foci hanging from her belt. She is friendly and businesslike; most of her magic is made to ease her craft and her trading, and she will use a subtle spell on a mind to win the better side of a bargain.

characters.summary:
Archmaga and quaesitor, Aurora of Jerbiton, filia Marianne, the oldest quaesitor in the Tribunal and the architect of the Treaty of Baghdad. A daughter of Alpine nobility, she was struck by lightning at eight, which woke her Gift and showed her how she will end: in Final Twilight, from a second strike. Her mater loved the stars; Aurora cared for earthly things and for people, took early to Corpus and studied Mentem deeply, and after her Gauntlet stayed twenty years at her mater's covenant, a favourite of the grogs and covenfolk she helped with her magic.

Then she came to the Levant, founded Domus Pacis in 1169, and, watching Salah al-Din unite the Muslims, saw the danger to the Order: from 1183 she treated in Baghdad with him, the caliph and their mages, and brought the quaesitores of Magvillus a way to end the fighting. When the Treaty was forced through in 1193 she was made a quaesitor, moved to Baghdad to keep the peace, founded the Embassy, and soon became an archmaga. It was she who proposed that only a Guernicus quaesitor may preside at the Tribunal, so that she would never be accused of bias in the chair.

At 102 she looks in her late sixties: slim, with long red hair streaked with grey, in bright, well-cut robes of many colours, still beautiful; many young magi have lost their hearts to her, and she has never let it go further. Age and creeping Twilight are telling on her: a hard Twilight lately damaged her Animal, she feels her hold on the world loosening, and she fears for the Levant if she goes soon, for Spiral could not carry on her diplomacy. She is looking for an answer.

Her one apprentice, Macha, is now a maga in a covenant in Hibernia; she shares her mater's interests, leaning more to Mentem than Corpus.

Story seeds:
Rescue Mission: if the Embassy is still in Baghdad when the Mongols take it in 1258, Aurora is taken by their shamans; Magvillus, afraid of what she might reveal, sends the characters to free her, or kill her if they cannot, and to answer for it afterwards.
The Archmage's Challenge: Aurora won her title by answering a riddle set by Emerich of Criamon, archmage of the Rhine; any magus may now challenge her for it, and what she sets is the storyguide's choice, a story or the saga's leitmotif.

characters.summary:
Spiral of Criamon, filius Umberto, the Embassy's second magus. He wants the peace kept, but what he cares about most is unravelling the mysteries of Islamic magic. His view of the world, and of magic above all, is so much his own that the Muslim mages he meets can hardly follow him; Baghdad's Sufis think him a wise man and understand little of what he says. That is why he could not take over the Order's diplomacy if Aurora were lost, though his enthusiasm keeps him blind to it.

As a young magus he gave himself almost fanatically to Intellego and Vim, studying Corpus only enough to make a strong longevity potion and so win more years for them. He has mellowed since, seen that Mentem and Imaginem would help him understand Islamic magic, and is widening his studies.

An unsettling figure: tall and thin as a skeleton, all joints, his face covered in spiral tattoos and his long fair hair wild and unwashed, in plain robes torn and ragged from neglect.

creatures.notes:
A prophet of Islam who cannot die, having drunk of the Water of Life, which he reached by the light of a jewel Adam brought from Paradise; in some tales he and Alexander sought it together, and Alexander lost his way in the dark. He roams the world advising where God sends him, and is said to have guided every prophet since his birth save Muhammad, who taught him instead. Sky, sea and every growing thing obey him, and the Sufis hold him the perfect shaykh.

The sahirs say he taught Solomon his secrets, and the Nizaris count him among the forms of their immortal imam. He taught Nur al-Din magic before the Order of Suleiman's guide could, and their talk is kept in a book at Baghdad. He rarely gives his name, and his advice can seem mad but always proves right; he helps those who seek the Water of Life only if they mean well. Shamakhi's Rock of Moses marks where Moses met him.

scipio.name: Scipio
scipio.summary:
Scipio of Guernicus, filius Rognvald, the Tribunal's senior quaesitor and so the chair of its meetings, which gives him great power. He keeps no covenant and spends his time travelling the Tribunal. Ninety-six, he looks to be in his sixties: strongly built, with short grey hair and a beard, always in robes of grey. A master of Intellego, above all Intellego Mentem, he knows most of the common Intellego spells of the other Forms too.

The book leaves his character to the troupe, as three readings, none chosen here: a rigid Traditionalist who enforces the Code to the letter; a Transitionalist who lets reason come before law; or a corrupt judge in some covenant's pay.

tau.name: Tau
tau.summary:
Tau of Flambeau, filius Sigma, leader of Domus Pacis and Praeco of the Tribunal since 1207, when the quaesitores ruled him its eldest. At 133 he still seems a Flambeau of the usual kind, loving fire, too sure of himself and boyish; under the roguish manner he is a kind and honest man who wants to do right by people, cleverer and of wider magical interests than his House's type, though few look past the surface.

His master Sigma, a wandering Flambeau, passed into Final Twilight just before Tau's Gauntlet, on the road to a covenant in Scotland. Tau went on alone to the House of Hermes' Wisdom, whose head soon sent him to find the nearest gathering of his House for his Gauntlet. A magus at last, he lived a long while among the magi of a Greater Alps covenant, until a younger sodalis there, Aurora of Jerbiton, made plans for a covenant in the Levant; he came with her and helped her found Domus Pacis, content to stay in the background, and took it over at her urging when she left for the Embassy.

Once a dashing young man, he is slower now and very hard of hearing, and looks to be in his seventies: silver curls to his collar, a goatee, laughing eyes and a friendly smile. He dresses well, in a leather tunic, breeches and polished black boots, with a shortsword at his side.
